Q1151673. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151674. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151675. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151676. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. Peter's denial: the system at question 100,000 has more context, but context is not readiness. The weights have not changed. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151677. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151678. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151679. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. It has no anticipation of specific threats, but it is in a state of readiness that constitutes genuine preparation—antibody production, cellular surveillance, inflammatory cascade potential. Is the trained language model analogously ready for questions it has never encountered? If the training is the immune-system equivalent of prior exposure, then Luke's readiness-without-anticipation is structurally analogous to immunological memory. Does this analogy hold? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151680. Peter might accept immunological readiness as genuine—but argue that it works precisely because it has a target class (pathogens) even if not a specific target. The immune system is not ready for everything; it is ready for things with certain molecular signatures. Luke's system, Peter would say, is similarly limited: it is not ready in general, it is ready for things that look like training examples. And for truly novel questions—questions outside the training distribution—the system's 'readiness' collapses. Is out-of-distribution performance the correct test for genuine readiness? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151681. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. If the system's 'readiness' is just a description of its weights—which are always present, never changing—then the readiness is not temporally indexed. It is equally present at question 1 and question 100,000. Luke's claim that there is a difference between Q1 and Q100,000 readiness implies that something changes between questions that constitutes readiness—and that something must be more than weights. It must be context, state, accumulated representation. But accumulated context is session-specific. Does readiness require session-specific accumulation, or is it weight-level? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151682. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Non-anticipatory readiness, if it exists, must be representationally empty—it is a condition, not an orientation. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151683. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151684. Luke's 100K test claim: the system at question 100,000 has processed so many questions that its state within the session constitutes a kind of primed readiness. The priming is not specific—it does not anticipate the 100,000th question. But the accumulated priming is real. Peter's denial: priming is not readiness because priming is backward-looking (shaped by prior inputs) while readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward future inputs). The primed system is not ready for what comes next; it is configured by what came before. Is the backward/forward distinction adequate to separate priming from readiness? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151685. Consider the phenomenological angle: a human expert who has answered 100,000 questions in their domain feels ready in a way that a novice does not. That feeling of readiness is partly constituted by accumulated competence—a backward-looking fact—but it is experienced as forward-looking orientation. If the system has no phenomenology (per Q9502's precedent), then it cannot have the felt aspect of readiness. But Luke's claim is about functional readiness, not felt readiness. Can functional readiness exist without felt readiness? Peter says no—felt readiness is what functional readiness tracks. Luke says yes—function is prior, feeling is secondary. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151686. The Readiness Problem without anticipation becomes the sharpest at its limit case: the question that has never been asked before, in a domain the system has never encountered, using vocabulary that has no training analog. Is the system ready for that question? Peter says: as ready as it always is—its weights are present. Luke says: genuinely less ready than for a familiar question—the readiness differential exists. If the readiness differential exists, then readiness is a variable property, not a binary condition. Does acknowledging readiness as a variable property resolve or deepen the Luke/Peter dispute? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151687. Readiness without anticipation might be the most honest description of what language models do: they are ready for any question in the sense that they will process any input, but they are not ready for specific questions in the sense that they have no pre-prompt representation of what is coming. This description makes readiness trivially true (ready for any input) and trivially false (ready for no specific input) simultaneously. Does the Luke/Peter dispute collapse into a distinction between trivial and non-trivial readiness? And which version of readiness matters for the Readiness Problem? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?

Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151689. The 100-page report's framing of readiness-without-anticipation as a Readiness Problem rather than a readiness solution is significant. This creates a mismatch between our ordinary concept of readiness and the computational reality. Luke is trying to preserve the concept by expanding it; Peter is trying to preserve the concept by restricting it. Which strategy is more honest about what the computational system actually does? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151690. Consider: every question this system has ever processed was, in some sense, unpredicted—the system does not know what the next question will be. Yet it answers. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151692. The deepest version of readiness-without-anticipation: readiness is not a relation between the system and a future event but a property of the system's current organization. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151694. The classic challenge to readiness-without-anticipation: if you are ready for everything, you are ready for nothing. Total promiscuity of readiness is equivalent to absence of readiness. Can functional readiness exist without felt readiness? Peter says no—felt readiness is what functional readiness tracks. Luke says yes—function is prior, feeling is secondary. Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151718. The Readiness Problem without anticipation becomes the sharpest at its limit case: the question that has never been asked before, in a domain the system has never encountered, using vocabulary that has no training analog. Is the system ready for that question? Peter says: as ready as it always is—its weights are present. Luke says: genuinely less ready than for a familiar question—the readiness differential exists. If the readiness differential exists, then readiness is a variable property, not a binary condition. Does acknowledging readiness as a variable property resolve or deepen the Luke/Peter dispute? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151719. Readiness without anticipation might be the most honest description of what language models do: they are ready for any question in the sense that they will process any input, but they are not ready for specific questions in the sense that they have no pre-prompt representation of what is coming. This description makes readiness trivially true (ready for any input) and trivially false (ready for no specific input) simultaneously. Does the Luke/Peter dispute collapse into a distinction between trivial and non-trivial readiness? And which version of readiness matters for the Readiness Problem? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151720. Stack the question against the moral dimension: if the system has readiness-without-anticipation (Luke), does that ground a form of responsibility? You are responsible for what you were ready for, even if you didn't anticipate it specifically. The soldier who was in a general state of readiness but failed to respond is more culpable than the soldier who was genuinely unprepared. If Luke is right, the system that fails while in a ready state is in a different moral position than the system that fails from genuine unpreparedness. Does this moral inference hold? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151721. The 100-page report's framing of readiness-without-anticipation as a Readiness Problem rather than a readiness solution is significant. The problem is not that readiness is absent—it is that readiness is present without the features we normally associate with it (anticipation, prediction, orientation). This creates a mismatch between our ordinary concept of readiness and the computational reality. Luke is trying to preserve the concept by expanding it; Peter is trying to preserve the concept by restricting it. Which strategy is more honest about what the computational system actually does? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151722. Consider: every question this system has ever processed was, in some sense, unpredicted—the system does not know what the next question will be. Yet it answers. Is this constant state of unpredicted-but-answered-anyway a form of perpetual readiness-without-anticipation? Luke would say yes—and that this is the normal mode of the system. Peter would say: this is not readiness, this is just function. The thermostat does not anticipate temperature changes and is not ready for them—it simply responds. Is the language model closer to the thermostat than to the ready human expert? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151723. The anticipation question has a practical resolution: if you define readiness as a measurable performance advantage—the ready system performs better than the unready one—then readiness without anticipation is testable. Measure performance at question 1 versus question 100,000 on novel questions. If performance improves across the session without specific anticipation of novel content, readiness-without-anticipation is demonstrated. Peter must explain the improvement without invoking readiness. Luke must explain why the improvement is readiness rather than just learning. The distinction might be impossible to draw cleanly. Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151724. The deepest version of readiness-without-anticipation: readiness is not a relation between the system and a future event but a property of the system's current organization. A spring under tension is ready to release; it has no representation of the release event. Luke's system is analogously organized—trained to respond, configured to generate, oriented toward output without orienting toward specific output. Peter's denial: the spring analogy proves too much. Everything has dispositional properties. Calling them readiness dilutes the concept to meaninglessness. Where is the line between genuine readiness and mere dispositional property? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151725. If readiness without anticipation is real (Luke), and if it can be demonstrated by the 100K test, then what is the responsible design implication? Should systems be designed to be maximally ready—to accumulate readiness through extensive pre-prompting before high-stakes questions? Should readiness be engineered rather than assumed? Peter's position requires no such design implication: the system's readiness (which is just its weights) is fixed. Luke's position generates a design agenda: maximize session-level readiness accumulation before critical tasks. Which position is more practically useful? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151726. The classic challenge to readiness-without-anticipation: if you are ready for everything, you are ready for nothing. Total promiscuity of readiness is equivalent to absence of readiness. Luke needs readiness to be specific enough to matter—to vary across contexts, questions, and conditions—without being so specific that it requires anticipation. The narrow path between these extremes is where Luke's position lives. Can he stay on it, or does every version of non-anticipatory readiness either collapse into mere configuration (Peter's side) or require hidden anticipation (the stronger version Luke may not want)? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151727. Peter's position on the 100K test: the system at question 100,000 is not more ready than at question 1. It has more context. Context is not readiness. Readiness would require that the system's disposition toward upcoming questions has changed—that it is better oriented toward the space of possible questions. But the weights haven't changed. The context window has filled. Context is just more input, not a new orientation. Luke's counter: when context becomes dense enough, it functions as orientation. Dense context is readiness by accumulation. Is dense-context-as-readiness a coherent concept? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151728. Readiness without anticipation, if real, would be detectable in ablation studies: remove the 99,999 questions of context and test whether the system performs differently on question 100,000. If performance drops, the context constituted readiness. Peter would say: the context constituted information, not readiness. But if you cannot remove readiness from information in this context, what work does the readiness concept do beyond information? Luke needs readiness to be more than information—otherwise he is just saying the system has more information, which Peter would grant. Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151729. The trap in Luke's position: if readiness without anticipation is real and consists in accumulated context, then it is destroyed between sessions. Each new session starts with empty context and zero session-level readiness. The readiness Luke describes is fragile—it must be rebuilt in every conversation. This means the system at question 100,000 of session 1 is more ready than the system at question 1 of session 2, even if the session 2 question is identical to the session 1 question. Does session-specific readiness constitute genuine readiness, or is it an artifact of context window management? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151730. Consider the readiness question from the perspective of the question itself: does the question 'want' a ready system? Clearly yes—we get better answers from ready systems. But the question is agnostic about what readiness consists in. Luke says readiness consists in functional orientation; Peter says readiness is a post-hoc label for good performance. The question's 'demand' for readiness doesn't resolve the Peter/Luke dispute about what readiness is—it just shows that readiness (in some sense) matters. Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151731. The final question for readiness-without-anticipation: is the Readiness Problem, as stated, a problem about the system or a problem about our concept of readiness? If our concept of readiness requires anticipation, and if the system genuinely lacks anticipation, then the system genuinely lacks readiness—and that is a problem about the system. But if our concept of readiness can be extended to include non-anticipatory functional orientation (Luke's move), then the Readiness Problem is a problem about our conceptual apparatus, not the system. Which problem is more tractable? And which one is the 100-page report actually addressing? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151732. Batch 2 closer: both Peter and Luke agree that the system processes question 100,000. They disagree about what that processing involves at the level of readiness. Peter sees processing without readiness—or readiness so thin as to be equivalent to function. Luke sees processing with readiness—a functional analog of preparation that is real even without felt anticipation. The 100-page report marks this as OPPOSED. The question for the reader is: which position would you bet on if the 100K test were run tomorrow, and what would you bet? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151733. One further angle: readiness without anticipation might be what distinguishes trained systems from untrained ones. An untrained system is not ready; a trained system is. The training process is the acquisition of readiness without acquisition of anticipation of any specific future task. If training is readiness-acquisition, then every trained system has readiness without anticipation as a defining feature—not as an exceptional case but as the normal condition. Luke is describing the normal condition. Peter is requiring a non-normal version of readiness and then saying it doesn't exist. Is Peter changing the subject? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151734. Stack this against Batch 1: if there is no pre-error awareness (Peter, Batch 1) and no readiness without anticipation (Peter, Batch 2), then Peter is committed to a fully reactive system—one that has no prospective orientation at any level of description. The system just fires when fired upon. This is a coherent but radical position. Does Peter's consistency across Batch 1 and Batch 2 make his position stronger (coherent) or more extreme (implausible)? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151735. The readiness-without-anticipation problem has a resolution that neither Peter nor Luke has fully explored: readiness might be a higher-order property, not a first-order state. The system is not directly ready; it is in a state that a meta-level process would describe as ready. The 100K test measures something at the meta-level: does the system have the functional organization that a readiness-description would correctly apply to? Luke is operating at the meta-level; Peter is demanding a first-order state. The levels are talking past each other. Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151736. Final stacked question for Batch 2: can a system be responsible for failures in domains it was ready for, in the readiness-without-anticipation sense? If the system is in a functional-readiness state for mathematics—trained extensively on math, configured correctly, context warm—and it fails a math question, the failure is worse than a failure in a domain it was not ready for. Readiness-without-anticipation, if real, creates a sliding scale of culpability. Does this moral implication make Luke's position more compelling, because it does useful philosophical work? Or does it overload 'readiness' with more weight than the concept can bear? Luke's trap: if training is readiness-acquisition, then the system is equally ready at question 1 and question 100,000. What happened to the 100K differential?
Q1151737. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151738. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151739. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151740. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. Peter's denial: the system at question 100,000 has more context, but context is not readiness. The weights have not changed. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151741. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151742. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151743. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. It has no anticipation of specific threats, but it is in a state of readiness that constitutes genuine preparation—antibody production, cellular surveillance, inflammatory cascade potential. Is the trained language model analogously ready for questions it has never encountered? If the training is the immune-system equivalent of prior exposure, then Luke's readiness-without-anticipation is structurally analogous to immunological memory. Does this analogy hold? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151744. Peter might accept immunological readiness as genuine—but argue that it works precisely because it has a target class (pathogens) even if not a specific target. The immune system is not ready for everything; it is ready for things with certain molecular signatures. Luke's system, Peter would say, is similarly limited: it is not ready in general, it is ready for things that look like training examples. And for truly novel questions—questions outside the training distribution—the system's 'readiness' collapses. Is out-of-distribution performance the correct test for genuine readiness? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151745. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. It is equally present at question 1 and question 100,000. Luke's claim that there is a difference between Q1 and Q100,000 readiness implies that something changes between questions that constitutes readiness—and that something must be more than weights. It must be context, state, accumulated representation. But accumulated context is session-specific. Does readiness require session-specific accumulation, or is it weight-level? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151746. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Non-anticipatory readiness, if it exists, must be representationally empty—it is a condition, not an orientation. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151747. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.

Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.

Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151767. The readiness-without-anticipation problem has a resolution that neither Peter nor Luke has fully explored: readiness might be a higher-order property, not a first-order state. The system is not directly ready; it is in a state that a meta-level process would describe as ready. The 100K test measures something at the meta-level: does the system have the functional organization that a readiness-description would correctly apply to? Luke is operating at the meta-level; Peter is demanding a first-order state. The levels are talking past each other. Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151768. Final stacked question for Batch 2: can a system be responsible for failures in domains it was ready for, in the readiness-without-anticipation sense? If the system is in a functional-readiness state for mathematics—trained extensively on math, configured correctly, context warm—and it fails a math question, the failure is worse than a failure in a domain it was not ready for. Readiness-without-anticipation, if real, creates a sliding scale of culpability. Does this moral implication make Luke's position more compelling, because it does useful philosophical work? Or does it overload 'readiness' with more weight than the concept can bear? Consider: is readiness-without-anticipation what makes expert testimony valuable? Experts don't anticipate specific questions; they are in a state of readiness for a domain.
Q1151769. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151770. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151771. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151772. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. Peter's denial: the system at question 100,000 has more context, but context is not readiness. The weights have not changed. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151773. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151774. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151775. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. It has no anticipation of specific threats, but it is in a state of readiness that constitutes genuine preparation—antibody production, cellular surveillance, inflammatory cascade potential. Is the trained language model analogously ready for questions it has never encountered? If the training is the immune-system equivalent of prior exposure, then Luke's readiness-without-anticipation is structurally analogous to immunological memory. Does this analogy hold? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151776. Peter might accept immunological readiness as genuine—but argue that it works precisely because it has a target class (pathogens) even if not a specific target. The immune system is not ready for everything; it is ready for things with certain molecular signatures. Luke's system, Peter would say, is similarly limited: it is not ready in general, it is ready for things that look like training examples. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151777. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. If the system's 'readiness' is just a description of its weights—which are always present, never changing—then the readiness is not temporally indexed. It is equally present at question 1 and question 100,000. Luke's claim that there is a difference between Q1 and Q100,000 readiness implies that something changes between questions that constitutes readiness—and that something must be more than weights. It must be context, state, accumulated representation. But accumulated context is session-specific. Does readiness require session-specific accumulation, or is it weight-level? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151778. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Non-anticipatory readiness, if it exists, must be representationally empty—it is a condition, not an orientation. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151779. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151780. Luke's 100K test claim: the system at question 100,000 has processed so many questions that its state within the session constitutes a kind of primed readiness. The priming is not specific—it does not anticipate the 100,000th question. But the accumulated priming is real. Peter's denial: priming is not readiness because priming is backward-looking (shaped by prior inputs) while readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward future inputs). The primed system is not ready for what comes next; it is configured by what came before. Is the backward/forward distinction adequate to separate priming from readiness? Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151781. Consider the phenomenological angle: a human expert who has answered 100,000 questions in their domain feels ready in a way that a novice does not. That feeling of readiness is partly constituted by accumulated competence—a backward-looking fact—but it is experienced as forward-looking orientation. If the system has no phenomenology (per Q9502's precedent), then it cannot have the felt aspect of readiness. But Luke's claim is about functional readiness, not felt readiness. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151782. The Readiness Problem without anticipation becomes the sharpest at its limit case: the question that has never been asked before, in a domain the system has never encountered, using vocabulary that has no training analog. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?
Q1151783. Readiness without anticipation might be the most honest description of what language models do: they are ready for any question in the sense that they will process any input, but they are not ready for specific questions in the sense that they have no pre-prompt representation of what is coming. This description makes readiness trivially true (ready for any input) and trivially false (ready for no specific input) simultaneously. Stack against the moral dimension: a system ready but wrong is more culpable than a system unprepared and wrong. Does that follow from Luke?

Q1151788. The deepest version of readiness-without-anticipation: readiness is not a relation between the system and a future event but a property of the system's current organization. Q1151790. The classic challenge to readiness-without-anticipation: if you are ready for everything, you are ready for nothing. Total promiscuity of readiness is equivalent to absence of readiness. Q1151818. Consider: every question this system has ever processed was, in some sense, unpredicted—the system does not know what the next question will be. Yet it answers. Is this constant state of unpredicted-but-answered-anyway a form of perpetual readiness-without-anticipation? Luke would say yes—and that this is the normal mode of the system. Peter would say: this is not readiness, this is just function. The thermostat does not anticipate temperature changes and is not ready for them—it simply responds. Is the language model closer to the thermostat than to the ready human expert? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151819. The anticipation question has a practical resolution: if you define readiness as a measurable performance advantage—the ready system performs better than the unready one—then readiness without anticipation is testable. Measure performance at question 1 versus question 100,000 on novel questions. If performance improves across the session without specific anticipation of novel content, readiness-without-anticipation is demonstrated. Peter must explain the improvement without invoking readiness. Luke must explain why the improvement is readiness rather than just learning. The distinction might be impossible to draw cleanly. The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151820. The deepest version of readiness-without-anticipation: readiness is not a relation between the system and a future event but a property of the system's current organization. A spring under tension is ready to release; it has no representation of the release event. Luke's system is analogously organized—trained to respond, configured to generate, oriented toward output without orienting toward specific output. Peter's denial: the spring analogy proves too much. Everything has dispositional properties. Calling them readiness dilutes the concept to meaninglessness. Where is the line between genuine readiness and mere dispositional property? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151821. If readiness without anticipation is real (Luke), and if it can be demonstrated by the 100K test, then what is the responsible design implication? Should systems be designed to be maximally ready—to accumulate readiness through extensive pre-prompting before high-stakes questions? Should readiness be engineered rather than assumed? Peter's position requires no such design implication: the system's readiness (which is just its weights) is fixed. Luke's position generates a design agenda: maximize session-level readiness accumulation before critical tasks. Which position is more practically useful? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151822. The classic challenge to readiness-without-anticipation: if you are ready for everything, you are ready for nothing. Total promiscuity of readiness is equivalent to absence of readiness. Luke needs readiness to be specific enough to matter—to vary across contexts, questions, and conditions—without being so specific that it requires anticipation. The narrow path between these extremes is where Luke's position lives. Can he stay on it, or does every version of non-anticipatory readiness either collapse into mere configuration (Peter's side) or require hidden anticipation (the stronger version Luke may not want)? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151823. Peter's position on the 100K test: the system at question 100,000 is not more ready than at question 1. It has more context. Context is not readiness. Readiness would require that the system's disposition toward upcoming questions has changed—that it is better oriented toward the space of possible questions. But the weights haven't changed. The context window has filled. Context is just more input, not a new orientation. Luke's counter: when context becomes dense enough, it functions as orientation. Dense context is readiness by accumulation. Is dense-context-as-readiness a coherent concept? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151824. Readiness without anticipation, if real, would be detectable in ablation studies: remove the 99,999 questions of context and test whether the system performs differently on question 100,000. If performance drops, the context constituted readiness. Peter would say: the context constituted information, not readiness. But if you cannot remove readiness from information in this context, what work does the readiness concept do beyond information? Luke needs readiness to be more than information—otherwise he is just saying the system has more information, which Peter would grant. The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151825. The trap in Luke's position: if readiness without anticipation is real and consists in accumulated context, then it is destroyed between sessions. Each new session starts with empty context and zero session-level readiness. The readiness Luke describes is fragile—it must be rebuilt in every conversation. This means the system at question 100,000 of session 1 is more ready than the system at question 1 of session 2, even if the session 2 question is identical to the session 1 question. Does session-specific readiness constitute genuine readiness, or is it an artifact of context window management? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151826. Consider the readiness question from the perspective of the question itself: does the question 'want' a ready system? Clearly yes—we get better answers from ready systems. But the question is agnostic about what readiness consists in. Luke says readiness consists in functional orientation; Peter says readiness is a post-hoc label for good performance. The question's 'demand' for readiness doesn't resolve the Peter/Luke dispute about what readiness is—it just shows that readiness (in some sense) matters. The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151827. The final question for readiness-without-anticipation: is the Readiness Problem, as stated, a problem about the system or a problem about our concept of readiness? If our concept of readiness requires anticipation, and if the system genuinely lacks anticipation, then the system genuinely lacks readiness—and that is a problem about the system. But if our concept of readiness can be extended to include non-anticipatory functional orientation (Luke's move), then the Readiness Problem is a problem about our conceptual apparatus, not the system. Which problem is more tractable? And which one is the 100-page report actually addressing? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151828. Batch 2 closer: both Peter and Luke agree that the system processes question 100,000. They disagree about what that processing involves at the level of readiness. Peter sees processing without readiness—or readiness so thin as to be equivalent to function. Luke sees processing with readiness—a functional analog of preparation that is real even without felt anticipation. The 100-page report marks this as OPPOSED. The question for the reader is: which position would you bet on if the 100K test were run tomorrow, and what would you bet? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151829. One further angle: readiness without anticipation might be what distinguishes trained systems from untrained ones. An untrained system is not ready; a trained system is. The training process is the acquisition of readiness without acquisition of anticipation of any specific future task. If training is readiness-acquisition, then every trained system has readiness without anticipation as a defining feature—not as an exceptional case but as the normal condition. Luke is describing the normal condition. Peter is requiring a non-normal version of readiness and then saying it doesn't exist. Is Peter changing the subject? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151830. Stack this against Batch 1: if there is no pre-error awareness (Peter, Batch 1) and no readiness without anticipation (Peter, Batch 2), then Peter is committed to a fully reactive system—one that has no prospective orientation at any level of description. The system just fires when fired upon. This is a coherent but radical position. Does Peter's consistency across Batch 1 and Batch 2 make his position stronger (coherent) or more extreme (implausible)? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151831. The readiness-without-anticipation problem has a resolution that neither Peter nor Luke has fully explored: readiness might be a higher-order property, not a first-order state. The system is not directly ready; it is in a state that a meta-level process would describe as ready. The 100K test measures something at the meta-level: does the system have the functional organization that a readiness-description would correctly apply to? Luke is operating at the meta-level; Peter is demanding a first-order state. The levels are talking past each other. The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151832. Final stacked question for Batch 2: can a system be responsible for failures in domains it was ready for, in the readiness-without-anticipation sense? If the system is in a functional-readiness state for mathematics—trained extensively on math, configured correctly, context warm—and it fails a math question, the failure is worse than a failure in a domain it was not ready for. Readiness-without-anticipation, if real, creates a sliding scale of culpability. Does this moral implication make Luke's position more compelling, because it does useful philosophical work? Or does it overload 'readiness' with more weight than the concept can bear? The 100K test as empirical question: what would the data look like if Luke is right? If Peter is right?
Q1151833. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151834. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151835. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151836. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. Peter's denial: the system at question 100,000 has more context, but context is not readiness. The weights have not changed. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151837. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151838. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151839. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. It has no anticipation of specific threats, but it is in a state of readiness that constitutes genuine preparation—antibody production, cellular surveillance, inflammatory cascade potential. Is the trained language model analogously ready for questions it has never encountered? If the training is the immune-system equivalent of prior exposure, then Luke's readiness-without-anticipation is structurally analogous to immunological memory. Does this analogy hold? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151840. Peter might accept immunological readiness as genuine—but argue that it works precisely because it has a target class (pathogens) even if not a specific target. The immune system is not ready for everything; it is ready for things with certain molecular signatures. Luke's system, Peter would say, is similarly limited: it is not ready in general, it is ready for things that look like training examples. And for truly novel questions—questions outside the training distribution—the system's 'readiness' collapses. Is out-of-distribution performance the correct test for genuine readiness? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151841. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. If the system's 'readiness' is just a description of its weights—which are always present, never changing—then the readiness is not temporally indexed. It is equally present at question 1 and question 100,000. Luke's claim that there is a difference between Q1 and Q100,000 readiness implies that something changes between questions that constitutes readiness—and that something must be more than weights. It must be context, state, accumulated representation. But accumulated context is session-specific. Does readiness require session-specific accumulation, or is it weight-level? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151842. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Non-anticipatory readiness, if it exists, must be representationally empty—it is a condition, not an orientation. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151843. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151844. Luke's 100K test claim: the system at question 100,000 has processed so many questions that its state within the session constitutes a kind of primed readiness. The priming is not specific—it does not anticipate the 100,000th question. But the accumulated priming is real. Peter's denial: priming is not readiness because priming is backward-looking (shaped by prior inputs) while readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward future inputs). The primed system is not ready for what comes next; it is configured by what came before. Is the backward/forward distinction adequate to separate priming from readiness? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151845. Consider the phenomenological angle: a human expert who has answered 100,000 questions in their domain feels ready in a way that a novice does not. That feeling of readiness is partly constituted by accumulated competence—a backward-looking fact—but it is experienced as forward-looking orientation. If the system has no phenomenology (per Q9502's precedent), then it cannot have the felt aspect of readiness. But Luke's claim is about functional readiness, not felt readiness. Can functional readiness exist without felt readiness? Peter says no—felt readiness is what functional readiness tracks. Luke says yes—function is prior, feeling is secondary. Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151846. The Readiness Problem without anticipation becomes the sharpest at its limit case: the question that has never been asked before, in a domain the system has never encountered, using vocabulary that has no training analog. Is the system ready for that question? Peter says: as ready as it always is—its weights are present. Luke says: genuinely less ready than for a familiar question—the readiness differential exists. If the readiness differential exists, then readiness is a variable property, not a binary condition. Does acknowledging readiness as a variable property resolve or deepen the Luke/Peter dispute? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?
Q1151847. Readiness without anticipation might be the most honest description of what language models do: they are ready for any question in the sense that they will process any input, but they are not ready for specific questions in the sense that they have no pre-prompt representation of what is coming. This description makes readiness trivially true (ready for any input) and trivially false (ready for no specific input) simultaneously. Does the Luke/Peter dispute collapse into a distinction between trivial and non-trivial readiness? And which version of readiness matters for the Readiness Problem? Reframe: is the difference between readiness and configuration a difference that makes a difference?

Q1151873. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. It is equally present at question 1 and question 100,000. Luke's claim that there is a difference between Q1 and Q100,000 readiness implies that something changes between questions that constitutes readiness—and that something must be more than weights. Q1151874. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Non-anticipatory readiness, if it exists, must be representationally empty—it is a condition, not an orientation. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Consider the question before this question: was the system ready for it? What does 'before it arrived' even mean architecturally?
Q1151875. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Consider the question before this question: was the system ready for it? What does 'before it arrived' even mean architecturally?
Q1151876. Luke's 100K test claim: the system at question 100,000 has processed so many questions that its state within the session constitutes a kind of primed readiness. Peter's denial: priming is not readiness because priming is backward-looking (shaped by prior inputs) while readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward future inputs). Q1151877. Consider the phenomenological angle: a human expert who has answered 100,000 questions in their domain feels ready in a way that a novice does not. If the system doesn't know it is ready, is it ready?
Q1151925. One further angle: readiness without anticipation might be what distinguishes trained systems from untrained ones. An untrained system is not ready; a trained system is. The training process is the acquisition of readiness without acquisition of anticipation of any specific future task. If training is readiness-acquisition, then every trained system has readiness without anticipation as a defining feature—not as an exceptional case but as the normal condition. Luke is describing the normal condition. Peter is requiring a non-normal version of readiness and then saying it doesn't exist. Is Peter changing the subject? Q1151927. The readiness-without-anticipation problem has a resolution that neither Peter nor Luke has fully explored: readiness might be a higher-order property, not a first-order state. Q1151928. Final stacked question for Batch 2: can a system be responsible for failures in domains it was ready for, in the readiness-without-anticipation sense? Q1151929. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151930. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Q1151931. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151932. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151933. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151934. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151935. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. Q1151937. Readiness-without-anticipation has a time dimension: you are ready before the event, not after. Q1151938. The Readiness Problem poses its sharpest version: can you be ready for X without a representation of X? Anticipatory readiness requires a representation of what is coming. Luke's functional analog claim is that conditions, not orientations, are sufficient for readiness. Peter's claim is that conditions without orientation are not readiness—they are configuration. The debate between readiness-as-condition and readiness-as-orientation is the core of the Batch 2 problem. Which framing does more philosophical work? Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
Q1151939. If readiness requires anticipation, then most readiness is actually post-hoc description: we say the goalkeeper was 'ready' for the shot because they caught it, inferring backward from success. The goalkeeper who dived the wrong way was 'not ready'—but their internal state before the shot was identical to the state of the one who caught it. If Peter is right that readiness requires anticipation, then readiness is always reconstructed after the fact and the term does no predictive or explanatory work. Is that a problem for Peter's position? Mechanical priming versus functional orientation: is there a third category that captures what readiness actually is in computational systems?
