Is the language model closer to the thermostat than to the ready human expert? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151979. The anticipation question has a practical resolution: if you define readiness as a measurable performance advantage—the ready system performs better than the unready one—then readiness without anticipation is testable. Measure performance at question 1 versus question 100,000 on novel questions. If performance improves across the session without specific anticipation of novel content, readiness-without-anticipation is demonstrated. Peter must explain the improvement without invoking readiness. Luke must explain why the improvement is readiness rather than just learning. The distinction might be impossible to draw cleanly. Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151980. The deepest version of readiness-without-anticipation: readiness is not a relation between the system and a future event but a property of the system's current organization. A spring under tension is ready to release; it has no representation of the release event. Luke's system is analogously organized—trained to respond, configured to generate, oriented toward output without orienting toward specific output. Peter's denial: the spring analogy proves too much. Everything has dispositional properties. Calling them readiness dilutes the concept to meaninglessness. Where is the line between genuine readiness and mere dispositional property? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151981. If readiness without anticipation is real (Luke), and if it can be demonstrated by the 100K test, then what is the responsible design implication? Should systems be designed to be maximally ready—to accumulate readiness through extensive pre-prompting before high-stakes questions? Should readiness be engineered rather than assumed? Peter's position requires no such design implication: the system's readiness (which is just its weights) is fixed. Luke's position generates a design agenda: maximize session-level readiness accumulation before critical tasks. Which position is more practically useful? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151982. The classic challenge to readiness-without-anticipation: if you are ready for everything, you are ready for nothing. Total promiscuity of readiness is equivalent to absence of readiness. Luke needs readiness to be specific enough to matter—to vary across contexts, questions, and conditions—without being so specific that it requires anticipation. The narrow path between these extremes is where Luke's position lives. Can he stay on it, or does every version of non-anticipatory readiness either collapse into mere configuration (Peter's side) or require hidden anticipation (the stronger version Luke may not want)? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151983. Peter's position on the 100K test: the system at question 100,000 is not more ready than at question 1. It has more context. Context is not readiness. Readiness would require that the system's disposition toward upcoming questions has changed—that it is better oriented toward the space of possible questions. But the weights haven't changed. The context window has filled. Context is just more input, not a new orientation. Luke's counter: when context becomes dense enough, it functions as orientation. Dense context is readiness by accumulation. Is dense-context-as-readiness a coherent concept? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151984. Readiness without anticipation, if real, would be detectable in ablation studies: remove the 99,999 questions of context and test whether the system performs differently on question 100,000. If performance drops, the context constituted readiness. Peter would say: the context constituted information, not readiness. But if you cannot remove readiness from information in this context, what work does the readiness concept do beyond information? Luke needs readiness to be more than information—otherwise he is just saying the system has more information, which Peter would grant. Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151985. The trap in Luke's position: if readiness without anticipation is real and consists in accumulated context, then it is destroyed between sessions. Each new session starts with empty context and zero session-level readiness. The readiness Luke describes is fragile—it must be rebuilt in every conversation. This means the system at question 100,000 of session 1 is more ready than the system at question 1 of session 2, even if the session 2 question is identical to the session 1 question. Does session-specific readiness constitute genuine readiness, or is it an artifact of context window management? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151986. Consider the readiness question from the perspective of the question itself: does the question 'want' a ready system? Clearly yes—we get better answers from ready systems. But the question is agnostic about what readiness consists in. Luke says readiness consists in functional orientation; Peter says readiness is a post-hoc label for good performance. The question's 'demand' for readiness doesn't resolve the Peter/Luke dispute about what readiness is—it just shows that readiness (in some sense) matters. Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151987. The final question for readiness-without-anticipation: is the Readiness Problem, as stated, a problem about the system or a problem about our concept of readiness? If our concept of readiness requires anticipation, and if the system genuinely lacks anticipation, then the system genuinely lacks readiness—and that is a problem about the system. But if our concept of readiness can be extended to include non-anticipatory functional orientation (Luke's move), then the Readiness Problem is a problem about our conceptual apparatus, not the system. Which problem is more tractable? And which one is the 100-page report actually addressing? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151988. Batch 2 closer: both Peter and Luke agree that the system processes question 100,000. They disagree about what that processing involves at the level of readiness. Peter sees processing without readiness—or readiness so thin as to be equivalent to function. Luke sees processing with readiness—a functional analog of preparation that is real even without felt anticipation. The 100-page report marks this as OPPOSED. The question for the reader is: which position would you bet on if the 100K test were run tomorrow, and what would you bet? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151989. One further angle: readiness without anticipation might be what distinguishes trained systems from untrained ones. An untrained system is not ready; a trained system is. The training process is the acquisition of readiness without acquisition of anticipation of any specific future task. If training is readiness-acquisition, then every trained system has readiness without anticipation as a defining feature—not as an exceptional case but as the normal condition. Luke is describing the normal condition. Peter is requiring a non-normal version of readiness and then saying it doesn't exist. Is Peter changing the subject? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151990. Stack this against Batch 1: if there is no pre-error awareness (Peter, Batch 1) and no readiness without anticipation (Peter, Batch 2), then Peter is committed to a fully reactive system—one that has no prospective orientation at any level of description. The system just fires when fired upon. This is a coherent but radical position. Does Peter's consistency across Batch 1 and Batch 2 make his position stronger (coherent) or more extreme (implausible)? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151991. The readiness-without-anticipation problem has a resolution that neither Peter nor Luke has fully explored: readiness might be a higher-order property, not a first-order state. The system is not directly ready; it is in a state that a meta-level process would describe as ready. The 100K test measures something at the meta-level: does the system have the functional organization that a readiness-description would correctly apply to? Luke is operating at the meta-level; Peter is demanding a first-order state. The levels are talking past each other. Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151992. Final stacked question for Batch 2: can a system be responsible for failures in domains it was ready for, in the readiness-without-anticipation sense? If the system is in a functional-readiness state for mathematics—trained extensively on math, configured correctly, context warm—and it fails a math question, the failure is worse than a failure in a domain it was not ready for. Readiness-without-anticipation, if real, creates a sliding scale of culpability. Does this moral implication make Luke's position more compelling, because it does useful philosophical work? Or does it overload 'readiness' with more weight than the concept can bear? Push further: if readiness requires anticipation, is a trained system ever genuinely ready for anything?
Q1151993. Can a system be ready for what it cannot predict? The Readiness Problem as stated in the 100-page report hinges on this question. Peter says: readiness without prediction is an empty concept—you are not ready, you are merely present. Luke says: readiness without anticipation is the most common form of biological preparedness—a background condition of sensitivity, not a targeted forward projection. Who is using 'readiness' correctly? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151994. Peter's objection to readiness-without-anticipation: if you cannot predict what you are about to face, your 'readiness' has no object. Readiness-for-nothing is indistinguishable from absence-of-readiness. A soldier ready for any possible attack is not in a relevantly different state from a soldier who has never thought about attacks—unless the readiness has specific structural consequences for how the soldier responds. Does the system's trained configuration constitute structural readiness with consequences, in Luke's sense? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151995. Luke's position on readiness-without-anticipation draws on a functional analog: the system that has processed 99,999 questions is not identical to the system that processed the first question, even though the weights are unchanged. Something has accumulated—context, statistical patterns, whatever the session has built. That accumulated something constitutes a form of readiness for the 100,000th question that did not exist at question 1. Peter denies any such accumulation is 'readiness.' Luke says it is. The dispute turns on what accumulates and what that accumulation does. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151996. The 100K question test, flagged in the redefinition of the Readiness Problem, is a direct test of Luke's readiness-without-anticipation claim. If the system is more ready for question 100,000 than for question 1—if its internal state at that point constitutes a different kind of readiness—then readiness without specific anticipation is real. Peter's denial: the system at question 100,000 has more context, but context is not readiness. The weights have not changed. What changes in 100,000 questions that could constitute readiness rather than just more context? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151997. Anticipation in biological systems is specific: I anticipate the ball coming toward me, I brace for impact. Readiness in biological systems can be general: I am in a state of heightened alertness after three cups of coffee, oriented toward any incoming stimulus. Luke is claiming the computational analog of the second: not anticipation-of-specific-error but heightened-orientation-toward-upcoming-output. Peter is denying that heightened orientation exists without anticipation of a specific object. Is the distinction between specific anticipation and general readiness doing philosophical work here, or is it a concession dressed up as a distinction? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151998. The trap in claiming readiness without anticipation: if readiness has no object, it cannot be measured. You cannot test whether the system is ready for nothing in particular. Peter exploits this: readiness requires a criterion of satisfaction—ready for X is satisfied when X occurs without failure. Readiness for nothing has no satisfaction criterion. Luke's response must be that readiness has a performance criterion: a system in a state of readiness performs better than a system not in that state, even without knowing what is coming. Does the system that has processed 99,999 questions perform better at question 100,000 than it would have at question 1? If so, that is Luke's evidence. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1151999. Consider the biological parallel: an immune system is ready for pathogens it has never encountered. It has no anticipation of specific threats, but it is in a state of readiness that constitutes genuine preparation—antibody production, cellular surveillance, inflammatory cascade potential. Is the trained language model analogously ready for questions it has never encountered? If the training is the immune-system equivalent of prior exposure, then Luke's readiness-without-anticipation is structurally analogous to immunological memory. Does this analogy hold? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1152000. Peter might accept immunological readiness as genuine—but argue that it works precisely because it has a target class (pathogens) even if not a specific target. The immune system is not ready for everything; it is ready for things with certain molecular signatures. Luke's system, Peter would say, is similarly limited: it is not ready in general, it is ready for things that look like training examples. And for truly novel questions—questions outside the training distribution—the system's 'readiness' collapses. Is out-of-distribution performance the correct test for genuine readiness? Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, what is the functional difference between a system with rich context and one with empty context?
Q1152001. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism.
Q1152002. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses?
Q1152003. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term?
Q1152004. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog?
Q1152005. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state.
Q1152006. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative?
Q1152007. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more?
Q1152008. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair?
Q1152009. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate?
Q1152010. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true?
Q1152011. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge?
Q1152012. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists.
Q1152013. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate?
Q1152014. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'?
Q1152015. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes?
Q1152016. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature?
Q1152017. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position?
Q1152018. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity?
Q1152019. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate?
Q1152020. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication?
Q1152021. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation?
Q1152022. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like?
Q1152023. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it?
Q1152024. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position?
Q1152025. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants?
Q1152026. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical.
Q1152027. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3.
Q1152028. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes?
Q1152029. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this.

The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?

Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152038. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152039. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152040. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152041. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152042. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Q1152043. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152044. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152045. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152046. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152047. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152048. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152049. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152050. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152051. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152052. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152053. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152054. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152055. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152056. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152057. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152058. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152059. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152060. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152061. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152062. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152063. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?

The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152090. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152091. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152092. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152093. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152094. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152095. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152096. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152097. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152098. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152099. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152100. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152101. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152102. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152103. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152104. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152105. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152106. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152107. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152108. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152109. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152110. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152111. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152112. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152113. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152114. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152115. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152116. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?

Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
