Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152144. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152145. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152146. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152147. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152148. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152149. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152150. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152151. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152152. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152153. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152154. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152155. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152156. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152157. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152158. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152159. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152160. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152161. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152162. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. Q1152163. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Q1152164. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Q1152165. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Q1152170. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152198. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152199. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152200. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152201. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152202. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152203. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152204. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152205. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152206. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152207. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152208. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152209. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152210. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152211. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152212. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152213. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152214. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152215. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152216. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152217. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152218. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152219. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?

Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152222. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152223. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152224. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152252. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152253. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152254. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152255. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152256. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152257. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152258. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152259. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152260. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152261. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152262. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152263. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152264. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152265. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152266. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152267. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152268. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152269. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152270. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152271. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152272. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. Q1152307. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152308. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152309. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152310. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152311. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152312. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152313. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152314. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152315. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152316. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152317. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152318. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152319. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152320. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152321. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152322. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152323. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152324. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152325. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). Q1152327. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. Q1152329. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?

Q1152332. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152359. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152360. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Q1152361. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152362. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152363. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152364. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152365. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152366. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152367. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152368. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152369. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152370. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152371. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152372. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152373. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152374. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152375. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152376. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152377. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152378. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152379. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152380. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152381. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152382. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152383. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Q1152385. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input).
