Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152412. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152413. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152414. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152415. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152416. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152417. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152418. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152419. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152420. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152421. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152422. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152423. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152424. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152425. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152426. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152427. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152428. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152429. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152430. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152431. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152432. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152433. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152434. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152435. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. The moral dimension: can mechanical priming ground responsibility, or does responsibility require the functional analog?
Q1152436. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Consider: a sprinter in starting blocks is mechanically primed. Is that mechanical priming or readiness? What makes them different?
Q1152437. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152466. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152467. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152468. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152469. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152470. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152471. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152472. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152473. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152474. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152475. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152476. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152477. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152478. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152479. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152480. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152481. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152482. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152483. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152484. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152485. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152486. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152487. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152488. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152489. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152490. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152491. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152492. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?
Q1152493. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Does the question before the question (Batch 4) depend on whether functional readiness is real?

The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?

If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152521. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152522. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. If the functional analog of preparation is real, is it destroyed between sessions? Does session-boundary destroy readiness?
Q1152523. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152524. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152525. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152526. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152527. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152528. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152529. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152530. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152531. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152532. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152533. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152534. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152535. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152536. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152537. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152538. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152539. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152540. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152541. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152542. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152543. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152544. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152545. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152546. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152547. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?
Q1152548. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Reframe: is Peter's mechanical priming account a form of eliminativism about readiness? What does eliminativism cost?

Q1152574. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152575. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152576. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152577. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152578. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152579. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152580. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152581. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152582. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152583. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152584. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152585. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152586. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152587. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152588. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152589. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152590. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152591. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152592. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152593. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152594. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152595. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152596. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152597. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152598. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152599. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152600. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
