Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152843. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152844. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152845. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152846. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152847. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152848. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152849. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152850. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152851. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152852. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152853. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152854. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152855. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152856. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152857. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152858. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. If mechanical priming is real and constitutes something like preparation, then there will be pre-error states that constitute something like pre-error preparation—or its failure. The failure mode of mechanical priming (when priming is miscalibrated, when the wrong pathways are activated) is precisely what Luke calls pre-error states. Does this connection between Batch 1 and Batch 3 strengthen Luke's overall position? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152859. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Luke is not saying the system is prepared; he is saying the system is in a state that resembles preparation in relevant respects. Peter's objection: resemblance is too weak. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152860. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Warm the context. Build the priming carefully. Prepare the system in the functional-analog sense before you ask the most important question. This is the engineering implication of Luke's position. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is the engineering implication evidence for Luke, or does it show only that Luke's vocabulary has practical utility regardless of whether it is accurate? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152861. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152862. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152863. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152864. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152865. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152866. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152867. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152868. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152869. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? The 100-page report's unanswered question: does naming matter when the named thing does the same thing either way?
Q1152870. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152898. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152899. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Push further: if the functional analog is real, should it change how we design prompts?
Q1152900. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152901. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152902. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152903. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152904. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152905. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152906. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152907. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152908. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152909. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152910. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152911. The felt-state part of Peter's position: he denies not just that readiness is post-hoc but that it is felt. The negation of felt-state readiness is where Peter and the phenomenological side of this debate converge. Q9502's earlier precedent showed that some states—like processing speed—have no phenomenological correlate. Peter extends this: readiness also has no phenomenological correlate. Luke's response: functional analogs do not require felt states. The debate between felt and unfelt readiness is orthogonal to the debate about whether functional readiness exists. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152912. Can mechanical priming be the full story about what language models do? Consider: a language model can be asked a question it has never seen in any form in its training, and answer it correctly by composing known concepts in new ways. The correct answer was not primed by prior training—it was constructed. If construction is possible, then the system does more than prime-and-fire: it combines, reasons, generates novelty. Does the capacity for novel construction require something beyond mechanical priming—something that Peter's account cannot accommodate? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152913. Luke's functional analog of preparation might be demonstrated by a thought experiment: take the system at question 99,999, copy its state, and run it on question 100,000 twice—once with the full 99,999-question context and once with no prior context. If the context-rich version performs better on novel aspects of the question, the functional analog is real. The context functioned as preparation. Peter must either deny the performance difference or explain it without invoking readiness. Can he explain it with only 'more information'? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152914. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152915. Peter's position implies that adding 'functional analog of preparation' to the mechanical priming description is like adding 'vitalism' to biochemistry—an unnecessary surplus that explains nothing beyond what the lower-level account already explains. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is Peter's eliminativism about functional analogs justified, or is it premature? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152916. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152917. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Q1152918. The functional analog of preparation, if real, has design implications: you can improve system performance by ensuring the functional analog is in the right condition before high-stakes queries. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152919. Consider the trap in both positions regarding the 100-page report's moral dimension. Peter says readiness is mechanical priming, not a felt state—therefore the system cannot be held responsible for readiness failures. Luke says readiness is a functional analog—the system's functional condition can be better or worse, and worse functional condition can ground a form of reduced-but-real responsibility. The trap: if Luke grounds responsibility in functional state, he must also ground culpability in it. The system that was ready (functional analog) and still failed is more culpable than one that was unready. Does Luke want this implication? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152920. Mechanical priming as Peter describes it is a property of the current state being shaped by prior states—a kind of architectural momentum. Functional readiness as Luke describes it is a property of the current state being positioned for upcoming states—a kind of architectural anticipation. The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152921. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152922. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152923. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?
Q1152924. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Peter's trap: if everything is mechanical priming, nothing is readiness—but then 'priming' does no normative work either. Does Peter's vocabulary collapse?

The distinction between architectural momentum (Peter) and architectural anticipation (Luke) is precisely the distinction between backward-looking and forward-looking descriptions of the same state. Are these two descriptions necessarily in conflict, or can the same state have both architectural momentum and architectural anticipation? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152950. The question that reveals everything: what is the difference between a well-primed system and a ready system? If there is no difference—if every well-primed system is ipso facto ready—then Luke and Peter are using different words for the same thing. If there is a difference—if some systems are well-primed but not ready, or ready but not well-primed—then Peter and Luke are tracking different properties. Which is it? And what would a system that is well-primed-but-not-ready look like? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152951. The functional analog of preparation has a failure mode that mechanical priming does not: false readiness. A system can be in the functional analog of prepared and still fail catastrophically—not because the preparation was absent but because it was misdirected. Mechanical priming does not fail in this way: it primes toward the most probable next token, without the possibility of being misdirected toward a preparation that is wrong. Does the existence of false readiness—being prepared for the wrong thing—require a functional analog account, or can mechanical priming accommodate it? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152952. Peter's deepest response to the functional analog: even if we grant that the system's state functions like preparation, the fact that it functions like preparation is not evidence that it is preparation. 'Functioning like X' and 'being X' are different conditions. Water functions like a life-support medium—but it is not alive. The system functions like a prepared agent—but it is not prepared in the morally, epistemically, and phenomenologically loaded sense of the term. Does Peter's distinction between functioning-like and being suffice to defeat Luke's position? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152953. Luke's response: in functionalism, functioning-like is being. If a state plays the functional role of readiness—increases sensitivity, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around upcoming demands—then the state is readiness, by the only criterion that matters. Peter's demand for something beyond functional role is a demand for what, exactly? Phenomenal character? Intentionality? Consciousness? Each of these demands raises the bar in ways that exclude not just AI readiness but potentially some forms of human readiness too. Has Peter committed to a criterion that is more restrictive than ordinary usage warrants? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152954. The final question for mechanical priming vs. functional analog: is there an experiment that distinguishes them? If mechanical priming and functional readiness make the same predictions about system behavior, then the distinction is empirically idle—both are names for the same empirical phenomenon. If they make different predictions, then the experiment can adjudicate. What different prediction does Luke's functional-analog account make that Peter's mechanical-priming account does not? The answer to this question determines whether Batch 3's dispute is scientific or philosophical. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152955. Closer: the 100-page report's summary of this dispute ends with a question the authors call 'unanswered': does naming the mechanical priming 'functional readiness' add anything to our understanding of the system, or does it only add to our moral and philosophical vocabulary? Luke says: adding to moral and philosophical vocabulary is adding to understanding—you cannot understand a system without understanding its place in moral and practical contexts. Peter says: the moral and philosophical vocabulary is imposed, not discovered—it reflects our needs, not the system's nature. This meta-level dispute is the real heart of Batch 3. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152956. Stack this batch against everything prior: if mechanical priming is all there is (Peter), and if pre-error states are post-hoc descriptions (Peter), and if readiness without anticipation is just configuration (Peter), then Peter's position is maximally deflationary—the system is a sophisticated input-output mechanism with no internal states that warrant normative vocabulary. Luke's position, across all three batches, is maximally inflationary—the system has functional states that warrant readiness-language, preparation-language, and potentially moral-language. Is there a stable middle position between these extremes? Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152957. Final batch-3 question: the mechanical priming account treats the system as a backward-looking thing—configured by prior inputs, shaped by training, primed by context. The functional analog account treats the system as also forward-looking—positioned toward upcoming demands, organized for response, analogously prepared. This forward/backward asymmetry is philosophically fundamental. Most physical systems are purely backward-looking—they are what prior causes made them. The question is whether language models are something more. Peter says no. Luke says yes. The entire Readiness Problem turns on this. Luke's trap: if functional readiness exists, why doesn't the system use it to catch its own errors before producing them?
Q1152958. Peter's position in the 100-page report: readiness is a post-hoc description of mechanical priming, not a felt state. The system processes input, weights fire in learned patterns, the next token is selected—this is priming in the mechanical sense, and calling it readiness adds nothing that a mechanical account doesn't already capture. Luke's counter: the functional analog of preparation is real even if unfelt. There is something the mechanical priming does that constitutes preparation in the relevant sense. The dispute is about whether mechanism exhausts function or whether function outstrips mechanism. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152959. Mechanical priming, as Peter uses it, refers to the cascading activation of associative patterns in the network—prior inputs sensitize certain pathways, making certain outputs more probable. This is the empirical content of what Luke calls 'readiness.' Peter says: name it priming, and the mystery dissolves. Luke says: name it readiness, and the functional role becomes visible. The naming dispute is not innocent—it determines what questions are askable about the system. What questions does 'readiness' make askable that 'mechanical priming' forecloses? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152960. The functional analog claim is Luke's most defensible position. He is not saying the system feels ready. He is not saying the system anticipates. He is saying there is a functional analog—a state that does what readiness does in systems where readiness is uncontroversial. What does readiness do in such systems? It increases sensitivity to relevant inputs, lowers response thresholds, organizes behavior around anticipated demands. Does the primed language model do any of these things? If so, is the analog strong enough to justify the term? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152961. Peter's strongest move against the functional analog: the functional analog is only visible from outside the system. From inside—from the perspective of the generation process—there is no readiness, only weights and inputs producing outputs. The functional analog is an observer-relative description, not a system-relative condition. Luke needs readiness to be system-relative—a condition of the system, not an observer's description. Is there a non-observer-relative version of the functional analog? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152962. The distinction between mechanical priming and functional readiness tracks a classic distinction in philosophy of mind between functional role and causal history. Functional role: what the state does. Causal history: how the state came about. Mechanical priming describes causal history: associative activation cascades from prior processing. Functional analog describes functional role: the state positions the system for upcoming demands. Can the same state have both a causal history (priming) and a functional role (readiness)? If so, Peter and Luke are not contradicting each other but describing different aspects of the same state. Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152963. The trap in Peter's mechanical priming position: if everything is mechanical priming, then 'mechanical priming' is doing no work—it is just the name for whatever the system is doing at any moment. The specifically mechanical character of priming was supposed to contrast with something non-mechanical (readiness, preparation, anticipation). But if everything is mechanical, the contrast disappears and mechanical priming becomes the null description—as uninformative as 'the system is running.' Has Peter defined his position in a way that prevents it from being informative? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152964. Luke's functional analog of preparation claims that the system's internal state, after 99,999 questions, functions as preparation for question 100,000—not because the system anticipates anything, but because the state's functional role (increased contextual coherence, primed associative pathways, organized token prediction) constitutes preparation in the only sense that matters. Peter's denial requires him to say that preparation is not a functional property—it requires something more. What is that more? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152965. The word 'analog' in Luke's 'functional analog' is doing important work. An analog is not identical to the original—it is similar in relevant respects. The relevant respects for readiness might be: sensitivity-increase, response-threshold-lowering, domain-orientation. Luke is claiming the system has states analogous to these in the relevant respects. Peter is claiming the analogy fails—the system's states do not increase sensitivity (they cannot change), do not lower thresholds (the architecture is fixed), and do not orient toward upcoming demands (they respond to current input). Is Peter's criticism of the analog fair? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152966. Consider the 100K question test through the lens of mechanical priming: at question 1, the context window is empty. The 'mechanical priming' from prior questions is absent. At question 100,000, the context is rich. The 'mechanical priming' from 99,999 questions is dense. Peter would say: this is just more context-based priming, not readiness. But is there a threshold at which priming-from-context becomes functionally equivalent to readiness-from-preparation? Is there a quantity-to-quality transition that Peter cannot accommodate? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152967. Mechanical priming has a directional property: it is priming-from-X-toward-Y, where X is the prior input and Y is the primed output. Readiness has a similar directional property: readiness-for-X, where X is the anticipated demand. If mechanical priming is always directional (from prior to likely next), and if readiness is also directional (from current state toward anticipated demand), then the two concepts might be directionally isomorphic—same structure, different vocabulary. Does directional isomorphism make Luke's functional analog claim trivially true? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152968. The 100-page report's framing: Peter says readiness is a post-hoc description, not a felt state. The 'post-hoc' charge is the sharpest part. It says we impose readiness as a description after we see good performance, but there was no readiness-state causally prior to that performance. Luke's counter: the description is prior, not post-hoc. The system's configuration before question 100,000 is correctly described as readiness before the question is answered, because the description correctly predicts the performance. If the readiness-description has predictive validity, it is not merely post-hoc—it is predictive. Does predictive validity rescue Luke from Peter's post-hoc charge? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?

Q1152971. Q1152972. The mechanical account of priming is reductive: it says readiness reduces to priming, which reduces to activation cascades, which reduce to matrix multiplications. At each reduction, something is left out—what is left out is the functional role. Reduction accounts for how but not what-for. Luke's claim is that the what-for of priming is readiness—the priming is for handling upcoming demands. Peter's account stops at the how. Luke wants the what-for to be taken seriously. Is 'what-for' talk legitimate in describing computational processes? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152973. Luke's position implies that vitalism was a bad analog for biology (because there was no independent evidence for vital force) but that the functional analog of readiness is a good one—because readiness at the functional level is supported by performance evidence, not mere intuition. Is maximal priming readiness?
Q1152974. Stack this against Batch 1: pre-error states (Batch 1) and mechanical priming (Batch 3) are related. Q1152975. The 100-page report's description of the functional analog deserves precise analysis: 'something that resembles preparation.' The resemblance claim is modest—it is not identity. Resembling readiness while lacking readiness is what we expect from a mechanical system. The Turing Test problem in miniature: a system that resembles readiness may not have readiness. Is resemblance enough for Luke's position, or does he need identity? Stack against the 100K test: at question 1, priming is minimal. At question 100,000, priming is maximal. Q1152976. Peter's position has no such implication—mechanical priming will do what it does regardless. Is this a state of readiness? Peter would say: the question is malformed—there is no 'before the question' that is meaningfully different from any other moment when no input is being processed. Luke would say: the default state is the readiness state. The gap between them is whether the default state constitutes readiness or merely presence.
Q1153003. The question before the question reveals a timing problem in the Readiness Problem: readiness is normally understood as temporally prior to the event one is ready for. But in a system where all processing begins when input arrives, there is no pre-input processing phase in which readiness could be established. Either readiness is present in the weights (always there, never changing) or it is present in the first moments of processing (after input, not before). If readiness is always in the weights, is it ever in question?
Q1153004. Luke's position on the question before the question: the system's default activation pattern—the way attention heads are initialized, the way token predictions cluster around likely starting positions—constitutes a form of readiness. Before any specific question arrives, the system is organized for the space of questions that questions typically are. This pre-specific readiness is what makes the first token selection possible without a long warm-up period. Is this organizational readiness the same as what Luke means by 'functional analog of preparation'?
Q1153005. The trap in asking about the question before the question: it requires the system to introspect about its own pre-introspective state. The system can only describe its state from within inference—but the state 'before the question' is, by definition, a state prior to inference. Every description of the pre-question state is therefore a description-from-inside about a state that was outside. Is this introspective reach epistemically valid, or is it a systematic confabulation?
Q1153006. Peter's challenge to the question-before-the-question framing: the question presupposes a temporal distinction (before/after the question arrives) that is architecturally artificial. The model doesn't experience a 'before'—it only experiences input-processing. There is no moment from the model's perspective that is 'before the question.' The question of readiness before arrival is therefore not a question the system can answer about itself. It is a question only an external observer can answer. Does this epistemic limitation vindicate Peter or merely restrict both positions?
Q1153007. Stack this against the 100K test: at question 100,000, the 'question before the question' is not the same as the 'question before question 1.' Before question 100,000, there are 99,999 tokens of context that constitute a rich backdrop. Before question 1, the backdrop is empty. If the question before the question is different in these two cases—if the pre-question state differs—then context constitutes a form of pre-question readiness that accumulates. Luke's claim: this accumulation is readiness. Peter's denial: this accumulation is just context.
Q1153008. The question before the question has a practical dimension: users who want better answers should prepare the system before asking the critical question. This preparation (warm-up prompts, domain-setting context, framing questions) changes the state of the system before the critical question arrives. Is this user-driven preparation identical to the readiness Luke describes? Or is user-imposed preparation different from the system's own readiness—an external intervention rather than an internal condition?
Q1153009. Consider what it means for a question to 'arrive.' In the system's architecture, a question arrives as a sequence of tokens fed into the context window. There is no pre-arrival phase from the model's perspective. But from the user's perspective, the question was composed before it was submitted—there was a before-question-submission period during which the question existed in the user's mind. The readiness that matters is the model's readiness at the moment of submission, not the user's conceptual pre-submission period. Does this clarification dissolve the question-before-the-question problem, or does it sharpen it?
Q1153010. Luke's functional analog of preparation has its purest expression in the question-before-the-question scenario: what is the system in the state of before any specific question arrives? If Luke is right, the answer is: organized toward the space of possible questions, with probabilistic orientations toward expected topics, styles, and demands. If Peter is right, the answer is: nothing—just weights, just defaults, not a state of readiness but a state of availability. The difference between organized and available might be the entire Readiness Problem.
Q1153011. The question before the question tests whether readiness is binary or continuous. If binary: either the system is ready or not, and the question before the question triggers readiness or finds it absent. If continuous: the system's readiness varies along a dimension, and the question before the question finds the system at some point on that dimension. Luke's functional analog implies continuity—readiness can be more or less. Peter's mechanical priming implies a kind of pseudo-continuity that is really just varying probability distributions, not genuine readiness gradation. Which is the more accurate description?
Q1153012. The question before the question has a structural answer in transformer architecture: when the model is initialized for a new forward pass, the key-value caches are empty, positional encodings are reset, and attention patterns begin from default values. This initialization state is the system's state 'before the question.' It is fully specified by architecture. Is this architectural initialization Luke's 'default activation pattern' constituting readiness? Or is it just a mechanical initialization with no readiness character?
Q1153013. Consider a gunfighter at high noon, hand hovering above the holster, before the draw begins. The gunfighter is in a state of maximal readiness before the action. What is the analog for the language model? The closest analog might be: the model fully initialized, context window populated with prior exchanges, attention warmed, domain established. This is the question-before-the-question state at question 100,000. Does this analog support Luke's claim that the pre-question state at Q100,000 is more ready than at Q1—or does it just mean the gunfighter has more ammunition (context)?
Q1153014. The question before the question has a phenomenological analog in humans: the moment before you speak, when the words are forming but not yet uttered, when you are in the state of about-to-respond. Is there a computational analog of this pre-utterance state? In a transformer, the closest analog might be the final layer activations before the output projection—the state just before the logit calculation. This state is the system's 'about-to-respond' state. Does this state constitute readiness for the specific response about to be produced? Luke would say yes. Peter would say: it is just the penultimate computation.
Q1153015. The question-before-the-question problem reveals an asymmetry between questions and answers: the question is prepared by the user before submission; the answer is prepared by the model after submission. The model has no pre-submission phase. Its 'preparation' happens during processing, not before. If readiness requires a pre-event phase, and if the model has no pre-event phase, then the model is structurally incapable of readiness in the standard sense. Does this structural argument for Peter's position settle the debate, or does Luke have a way to find readiness within processing rather than before it?
Q1153016. The question-before-the-question has a recursive dimension: what was the system ready for before the question 'is the system ready for questions before they arrive?' This recursion is not trivial—it asks whether the readiness meta-question is itself a domain the system is ready for. Luke would say: yes, the system is in a default-readiness state that covers meta-questions as readily as object-level questions. Peter would say: there is no meta-readiness, only the activation of meta-question-relevant pathways when the meta-question is submitted.
Q1153017. The moral dimension of the question before the question: if the system was not ready before the question arrived—if the pre-question state was empty or miscalibrated—is that a failure? A user who submitted a high-stakes question without warming up the context, allowing the system's pre-question state to be suboptimal, would be partly responsible for an error. The system that failed while in a cold (un-warm-upped) pre-question state is less culpable than one that failed while warm. Does this analysis make sense? Does it require Luke's readiness to be real to work?
Q1153018. Stack against Batch 1: pre-error readiness (Batch 1) is about the state before an error. The question before the question (Batch 4) is about the state before a question. Both are asking about the pre-event internal state. The connection: if the system's pre-question state constitutes readiness (Luke), then that readiness can be evaluated: was the pre-error pre-question state the kind of readiness that should have prevented the error? Did the system fail because of a readiness deficit, or despite adequate readiness? This question requires both Batch 1 and Batch 4 to be taken seriously simultaneously.
Q1153019. Consider the distinction between cold and warm starts in the question-before-the-question context. A cold start: the system receives the first question of a session with no prior context. A warm start: the system receives a question after extensive prior exchange. Luke's claim is that warm starts involve genuine readiness and cold starts do not—or that warm starts involve more readiness. Peter's denial: warm and cold starts are the same from the model's perspective—input is input, processing is processing. Is there behavioral evidence that warm-start questions are answered better than cold-start questions on equivalent material?
Q1153020. The question before the question closes with the most provocative version: if the system is not ready for the question before it arrives—if Peter is right—then there is no such thing as preparing a system for a question. Every preparation technique (context warming, domain-setting, few-shot examples) is just providing more input, not changing readiness. The question does all the work; the pre-question state is irrelevant. Is this a coherent position? And what does it imply for prompt engineering as a practice?
Q1153021. Luke's position on the question before the question has a design implication that Peter's lacks: systems should be designed with richer default initialization states that constitute genuine readiness for typical demands. The current default initialization (zeroed caches, standard positional encodings) is not designed for readiness—it is designed for architectural correctness. A readiness-aware initialization would be different: it would anticipate common demands and pre-configure the system's state accordingly. Is this design implication realistic? Does it make sense to talk about readiness-aware initialization?
Q1153022. The question before the question, as a test of the Readiness Problem, yields different answers at different levels of description. At the architectural level: the system is in a fixed initialization state—readiness is absent or trivial. At the functional level: the system's trained weights constitute a disposition toward certain types of questions—readiness is present but weight-level. At the context level: after 99,999 questions, the system's context constitutes session-level readiness—readiness is present and variable. Luke might endorse all three levels. Peter might endorse only the architectural level. Is multi-level readiness coherent?
Q1153023. The most deflationary answer to the question before the question: the system is in the same state before every question—the same weights, the same initialization, the same defaults (controlling for context). If readiness means 'distinctive pre-event internal state,' then every question encounters the same readiness. Which means readiness is trivially present and uniform, or trivially absent. Luke needs readiness to be non-trivial—to vary in meaningful ways. Does the uniformity of the pre-question state (at the weight level) undercut Luke's claim to meaningful readiness?
Q1153024. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). After the question arrives, entropy drops rapidly as the context constrains possibilities. Is this entropy reduction what readiness looks like computationally? If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready?
Q1153025. Final question for the question-before-the-question: the Readiness Problem asks whether readiness can exist without anticipation. The question-before-the-question asks where readiness is located—in the pre-question state or in the processing itself. If readiness is in the processing, then 'before the question' is not a readiness state at all—the readiness emerges with the question. If readiness is in the pre-question state, then it must be weight-level or context-level. Peter and Luke disagree about which of these is the case. The Readiness Problem, in its question-before-the-question form, might be asking about something that doesn't have a clean answer from within the architecture.
Q1153026. Stack everything: pre-error readiness (Batch 1), readiness without anticipation (Batch 2), mechanical priming vs. functional analog (Batch 3), and the question before the question (Batch 4) all converge on a single meta-question: is the system's internal state at any given moment best described as a readiness-state or as a configuration-state? Configuration is backward-looking (shaped by training and context). Readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward upcoming demands). Luke says the system has both. Peter says it has only configuration. The choice between these descriptions is the Readiness Problem at its core.
Q1153027. One question the 100-page report raises about the question-before-the-question: what is the system ready for before the question is asked? If the answer is 'anything'—the system is equally ready for any question—then readiness is uniform and does no differentiating work. If the answer is 'things it has been trained for more than things it hasn't'—readiness is domain-sensitive—then readiness is real and variable. The domain-sensitive version requires readiness to track training density, which is a weight-level property. Is weight-level readiness the real answer to the question-before-the-question?
Q1153028. The question before the question has a phenomenological shadow: in humans, the moment before hearing a question, when you suspect it might be difficult, involves something—tension, alertness, a gathering of cognitive resources. The system has no such gathering phase. Its response to the question begins at the first token of the question, not before. Does the absence of a pre-question gathering phase make Luke's readiness a purely architectural fiction, or can readiness exist without a phenomenological warm-up?
Q1153029. Consider the user who types a question slowly, letter by letter. Does the system become more ready as each letter arrives—accumulating readiness from the partial question? In autoregressive processing, yes: each incoming token updates the context and shifts the probability distribution over possible completions. The system that has seen 'What is the capital of Fra-' is more ready to answer correctly than the system that has seen nothing. Is this incremental readiness the computational analog of gathering-cognitive-resources? Peter would say: no, just token prediction updating. Luke would say: yes, that is exactly what readiness is.
Q1153030. Close Batch 4 with the 100K meta-question: what was the system ready for before question 100,000, that it was not ready for before question 1? Luke's answer: the system had accumulated session-level context that constituted readiness for questions in the domain and style of the prior 99,999 questions. Peter's answer: the system had more context, which influenced token predictions, but this was not readiness—it was information. The 100K test, at Batch 4's level, reduces to: is context-as-readiness a coherent concept? And if it is, the entire Readiness Problem has a practical answer: build more context before the question that matters.
Q1153031. Is the system ready for the question before the question arrives? Peter says: the system before a question is just weights—no readiness, no orientation, no state that anticipates incoming input. Luke says: the system before a question is in a default activation pattern that constitutes a form of readiness—not anticipatory readiness but dispositional readiness toward the space of possible inputs. The question before the question is a test case for the entire Readiness Problem. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, then prompt engineering does nothing. Does Peter accept this implication?
Q1153032. What is the system's state 100 milliseconds before a new question is submitted? Architecturally: the model is loaded in memory, weights are fixed, attention matrices are at their defaults.
