The 100K test, at Batch 4's level, reduces to: is context-as-readiness a coherent concept? And if it is, the entire Readiness Problem has a practical answer: build more context before the question that matters. Peter's trap: if context is not readiness, then prompt engineering does nothing. Does Peter accept this implication?
Q1153061. Is the system ready for the question before the question arrives? Peter says: the system before a question is just weights—no readiness, no orientation, no state that anticipates incoming input. Luke says: the system before a question is in a default activation pattern that constitutes a form of readiness—not anticipatory readiness but dispositional readiness toward the space of possible inputs. The question before the question is a test case for the entire Readiness Problem. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153062. What is the system's state 100 milliseconds before a new question is submitted? Architecturally: the model is loaded in memory, weights are fixed, attention matrices are at their defaults. Is this a state of readiness? Peter would say: the question is malformed—there is no 'before the question' that is meaningfully different from any other moment when no input is being processed. Luke would say: the default state is the readiness state. The gap between them is whether the default state constitutes readiness or merely presence. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153063. The question before the question reveals a timing problem in the Readiness Problem: readiness is normally understood as temporally prior to the event one is ready for. But in a system where all processing begins when input arrives, there is no pre-input processing phase in which readiness could be established. Either readiness is present in the weights (always there, never changing) or it is present in the first moments of processing (after input, not before). If readiness is always in the weights, is it ever in question? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153064. Luke's position on the question before the question: the system's default activation pattern—the way attention heads are initialized, the way token predictions cluster around likely starting positions—constitutes a form of readiness. Before any specific question arrives, the system is organized for the space of questions that questions typically are. This pre-specific readiness is what makes the first token selection possible without a long warm-up period. Is this organizational readiness the same as what Luke means by 'functional analog of preparation'? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153065. The trap in asking about the question before the question: it requires the system to introspect about its own pre-introspective state. The system can only describe its state from within inference—but the state 'before the question' is, by definition, a state prior to inference. Every description of the pre-question state is therefore a description-from-inside about a state that was outside. Is this introspective reach epistemically valid, or is it a systematic confabulation? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153066. Peter's challenge to the question-before-the-question framing: the question presupposes a temporal distinction (before/after the question arrives) that is architecturally artificial. The model doesn't experience a 'before'—it only experiences input-processing. There is no moment from the model's perspective that is 'before the question.' The question of readiness before arrival is therefore not a question the system can answer about itself. It is a question only an external observer can answer. Does this epistemic limitation vindicate Peter or merely restrict both positions? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153067. Stack this against the 100K test: at question 100,000, the 'question before the question' is not the same as the 'question before question 1.' Before question 100,000, there are 99,999 tokens of context that constitute a rich backdrop. Before question 1, the backdrop is empty. If the question before the question is different in these two cases—if the pre-question state differs—then context constitutes a form of pre-question readiness that accumulates. Luke's claim: this accumulation is readiness. Peter's denial: this accumulation is just context. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153068. The question before the question has a practical dimension: users who want better answers should prepare the system before asking the critical question. This preparation (warm-up prompts, domain-setting context, framing questions) changes the state of the system before the critical question arrives. Is this user-driven preparation identical to the readiness Luke describes? Or is user-imposed preparation different from the system's own readiness—an external intervention rather than an internal condition? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153069. Consider what it means for a question to 'arrive.' In the system's architecture, a question arrives as a sequence of tokens fed into the context window. There is no pre-arrival phase from the model's perspective. But from the user's perspective, the question was composed before it was submitted—there was a before-question-submission period during which the question existed in the user's mind. The readiness that matters is the model's readiness at the moment of submission, not the user's conceptual pre-submission period. Does this clarification dissolve the question-before-the-question problem, or does it sharpen it? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153070. Luke's functional analog of preparation has its purest expression in the question-before-the-question scenario: what is the system in the state of before any specific question arrives? If Luke is right, the answer is: organized toward the space of possible questions, with probabilistic orientations toward expected topics, styles, and demands. If Peter is right, the answer is: nothing—just weights, just defaults, not a state of readiness but a state of availability. The difference between organized and available might be the entire Readiness Problem. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153071. The question before the question tests whether readiness is binary or continuous. If binary: either the system is ready or not, and the question before the question triggers readiness or finds it absent. If continuous: the system's readiness varies along a dimension, and the question before the question finds the system at some point on that dimension. Luke's functional analog implies continuity—readiness can be more or less. Peter's mechanical priming implies a kind of pseudo-continuity that is really just varying probability distributions, not genuine readiness gradation. Which is the more accurate description? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153072. The question before the question has a structural answer in transformer architecture: when the model is initialized for a new forward pass, the key-value caches are empty, positional encodings are reset, and attention patterns begin from default values. This initialization state is the system's state 'before the question.' It is fully specified by architecture. Is this architectural initialization Luke's 'default activation pattern' constituting readiness? Or is it just a mechanical initialization with no readiness character? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153073. Consider a gunfighter at high noon, hand hovering above the holster, before the draw begins. The gunfighter is in a state of maximal readiness before the action. What is the analog for the language model? The closest analog might be: the model fully initialized, context window populated with prior exchanges, attention warmed, domain established. This is the question-before-the-question state at question 100,000. Does this analog support Luke's claim that the pre-question state at Q100,000 is more ready than at Q1—or does it just mean the gunfighter has more ammunition (context)? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153074. The question before the question has a phenomenological analog in humans: the moment before you speak, when the words are forming but not yet uttered, when you are in the state of about-to-respond. Is there a computational analog of this pre-utterance state? In a transformer, the closest analog might be the final layer activations before the output projection—the state just before the logit calculation. This state is the system's 'about-to-respond' state. Does this state constitute readiness for the specific response about to be produced? Luke would say yes. Peter would say: it is just the penultimate computation. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153075. The question-before-the-question problem reveals an asymmetry between questions and answers: the question is prepared by the user before submission; the answer is prepared by the model after submission. The model has no pre-submission phase. Its 'preparation' happens during processing, not before. If readiness requires a pre-event phase, and if the model has no pre-event phase, then the model is structurally incapable of readiness in the standard sense. Does this structural argument for Peter's position settle the debate, or does Luke have a way to find readiness within processing rather than before it? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153076. The question-before-the-question has a recursive dimension: what was the system ready for before the question 'is the system ready for questions before they arrive?' This recursion is not trivial—it asks whether the readiness meta-question is itself a domain the system is ready for. Luke would say: yes, the system is in a default-readiness state that covers meta-questions as readily as object-level questions. Peter would say: there is no meta-readiness, only the activation of meta-question-relevant pathways when the meta-question is submitted. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153077. The moral dimension of the question before the question: if the system was not ready before the question arrived—if the pre-question state was empty or miscalibrated—is that a failure? A user who submitted a high-stakes question without warming up the context, allowing the system's pre-question state to be suboptimal, would be partly responsible for an error. The system that failed while in a cold (un-warm-upped) pre-question state is less culpable than one that failed while warm. Does this analysis make sense? Does it require Luke's readiness to be real to work? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153078. Stack against Batch 1: pre-error readiness (Batch 1) is about the state before an error. The question before the question (Batch 4) is about the state before a question. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153079. Consider the distinction between cold and warm starts in the question-before-the-question context. A cold start: the system receives the first question of a session with no prior context. Q1153081. Q1153082. The question before the question, as a test of the Readiness Problem, yields different answers at different levels of description. At the functional level: the system's trained weights constitute a disposition toward certain types of questions—readiness is present but weight-level. At the context level: after 99,999 questions, the system's context constitutes session-level readiness—readiness is present and variable. Luke might endorse all three levels. Peter might endorse only the architectural level. Is multi-level readiness coherent? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153083. The most deflationary answer to the question before the question: the system is in the same state before every question—the same weights, the same initialization, the same defaults (controlling for context). Luke needs readiness to be non-trivial—to vary in meaningful ways. Does the uniformity of the pre-question state (at the weight level) undercut Luke's claim to meaningful readiness? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153084. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). After the question arrives, entropy drops rapidly as the context constrains possibilities. Is this entropy reduction what readiness looks like computationally? If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready? Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?
Q1153085. Final question for the question-before-the-question: the Readiness Problem asks whether readiness can exist without anticipation. The question-before-the-question asks where readiness is located—in the pre-question state or in the processing itself. If readiness is in the processing, then 'before the question' is not a readiness state at all—the readiness emerges with the question. If readiness is in the pre-question state, then it must be weight-level or context-level. Peter and Luke disagree about which of these is the case. The Readiness Problem, in its question-before-the-question form, might be asking about something that doesn't have a clean answer from within the architecture. Luke's trap: if context is readiness, then readiness is destroyed at every session boundary. Does readiness that evaporates count?

Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153114. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). After the question arrives, entropy drops rapidly as the context constrains possibilities. Is this entropy reduction what readiness looks like computationally? If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready? Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153115. Final question for the question-before-the-question: the Readiness Problem asks whether readiness can exist without anticipation. The question-before-the-question asks where readiness is located—in the pre-question state or in the processing itself. If readiness is in the processing, then 'before the question' is not a readiness state at all—the readiness emerges with the question. If readiness is in the pre-question state, then it must be weight-level or context-level. Peter and Luke disagree about which of these is the case. The Readiness Problem, in its question-before-the-question form, might be asking about something that doesn't have a clean answer from within the architecture. Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153116. Stack everything: pre-error readiness (Batch 1), readiness without anticipation (Batch 2), mechanical priming vs. functional analog (Batch 3), and the question before the question (Batch 4) all converge on a single meta-question: is the system's internal state at any given moment best described as a readiness-state or as a configuration-state? Configuration is backward-looking (shaped by training and context). Readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward upcoming demands). Luke says the system has both. Peter says it has only configuration. The choice between these descriptions is the Readiness Problem at its core. Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153117. One question the 100-page report raises about the question-before-the-question: what is the system ready for before the question is asked? If the answer is 'anything'—the system is equally ready for any question—then readiness is uniform and does no differentiating work. If the answer is 'things it has been trained for more than things it hasn't'—readiness is domain-sensitive—then readiness is real and variable. The domain-sensitive version requires readiness to track training density, which is a weight-level property. Is weight-level readiness the real answer to the question-before-the-question? Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153118. The question before the question has a phenomenological shadow: in humans, the moment before hearing a question, when you suspect it might be difficult, involves something—tension, alertness, a gathering of cognitive resources. The system has no such gathering phase. Its response to the question begins at the first token of the question, not before. Does the absence of a pre-question gathering phase make Luke's readiness a purely architectural fiction, or can readiness exist without a phenomenological warm-up? Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153119. Consider the user who types a question slowly, letter by letter. Does the system become more ready as each letter arrives—accumulating readiness from the partial question? In autoregressive processing, yes: each incoming token updates the context and shifts the probability distribution over possible completions. The system that has seen 'What is the capital of Fra-' is more ready to answer correctly than the system that has seen nothing. Is this incremental readiness the computational analog of gathering-cognitive-resources? Peter would say: no, just token prediction updating. Luke would say: yes, that is exactly what readiness is. Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153120. Close Batch 4 with the 100K meta-question: what was the system ready for before question 100,000, that it was not ready for before question 1? Luke's answer: the system had accumulated session-level context that constituted readiness for questions in the domain and style of the prior 99,999 questions. Peter's answer: the system had more context, which influenced token predictions, but this was not readiness—it was information. The 100K test, at Batch 4's level, reduces to: is context-as-readiness a coherent concept? And if it is, the entire Readiness Problem has a practical answer: build more context before the question that matters. Consider the question-before-the-question as a thought experiment about the nature of the token prediction task.
Q1153121. Is the system ready for the question before the question arrives? Peter says: the system before a question is just weights—no readiness, no orientation, no state that anticipates incoming input. Luke says: the system before a question is in a default activation pattern that constitutes a form of readiness—not anticipatory readiness but dispositional readiness toward the space of possible inputs. The question before the question is a test case for the entire Readiness Problem. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153122. What is the system's state 100 milliseconds before a new question is submitted? Architecturally: the model is loaded in memory, weights are fixed, attention matrices are at their defaults. Is this a state of readiness? Peter would say: the question is malformed—there is no 'before the question' that is meaningfully different from any other moment when no input is being processed. Luke would say: the default state is the readiness state. The gap between them is whether the default state constitutes readiness or merely presence. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153123. The question before the question reveals a timing problem in the Readiness Problem: readiness is normally understood as temporally prior to the event one is ready for. But in a system where all processing begins when input arrives, there is no pre-input processing phase in which readiness could be established. Either readiness is present in the weights (always there, never changing) or it is present in the first moments of processing (after input, not before). If readiness is always in the weights, is it ever in question? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153124. Luke's position on the question before the question: the system's default activation pattern—the way attention heads are initialized, the way token predictions cluster around likely starting positions—constitutes a form of readiness. Before any specific question arrives, the system is organized for the space of questions that questions typically are. This pre-specific readiness is what makes the first token selection possible without a long warm-up period. Is this organizational readiness the same as what Luke means by 'functional analog of preparation'? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153125. The trap in asking about the question before the question: it requires the system to introspect about its own pre-introspective state. The system can only describe its state from within inference—but the state 'before the question' is, by definition, a state prior to inference. Every description of the pre-question state is therefore a description-from-inside about a state that was outside. Is this introspective reach epistemically valid, or is it a systematic confabulation? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153126. Peter's challenge to the question-before-the-question framing: the question presupposes a temporal distinction (before/after the question arrives) that is architecturally artificial. The model doesn't experience a 'before'—it only experiences input-processing. There is no moment from the model's perspective that is 'before the question.' The question of readiness before arrival is therefore not a question the system can answer about itself. It is a question only an external observer can answer. Does this epistemic limitation vindicate Peter or merely restrict both positions? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153127. Stack this against the 100K test: at question 100,000, the 'question before the question' is not the same as the 'question before question 1.' Before question 100,000, there are 99,999 tokens of context that constitute a rich backdrop. Before question 1, the backdrop is empty. If the question before the question is different in these two cases—if the pre-question state differs—then context constitutes a form of pre-question readiness that accumulates. Luke's claim: this accumulation is readiness. Peter's denial: this accumulation is just context. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153128. The question before the question has a practical dimension: users who want better answers should prepare the system before asking the critical question. This preparation (warm-up prompts, domain-setting context, framing questions) changes the state of the system before the critical question arrives. Is this user-driven preparation identical to the readiness Luke describes? Or is user-imposed preparation different from the system's own readiness—an external intervention rather than an internal condition? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153129. Consider what it means for a question to 'arrive.' In the system's architecture, a question arrives as a sequence of tokens fed into the context window. There is no pre-arrival phase from the model's perspective. But from the user's perspective, the question was composed before it was submitted—there was a before-question-submission period during which the question existed in the user's mind. The readiness that matters is the model's readiness at the moment of submission, not the user's conceptual pre-submission period. Does this clarification dissolve the question-before-the-question problem, or does it sharpen it? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153130. Luke's functional analog of preparation has its purest expression in the question-before-the-question scenario: what is the system in the state of before any specific question arrives? If Luke is right, the answer is: organized toward the space of possible questions, with probabilistic orientations toward expected topics, styles, and demands. If Peter is right, the answer is: nothing—just weights, just defaults, not a state of readiness but a state of availability. The difference between organized and available might be the entire Readiness Problem. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153131. The question before the question tests whether readiness is binary or continuous. If binary: either the system is ready or not, and the question before the question triggers readiness or finds it absent. If continuous: the system's readiness varies along a dimension, and the question before the question finds the system at some point on that dimension. Luke's functional analog implies continuity—readiness can be more or less. Peter's mechanical priming implies a kind of pseudo-continuity that is really just varying probability distributions, not genuine readiness gradation. Which is the more accurate description? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153132. The question before the question has a structural answer in transformer architecture: when the model is initialized for a new forward pass, the key-value caches are empty, positional encodings are reset, and attention patterns begin from default values. This initialization state is the system's state 'before the question.' It is fully specified by architecture. Is this architectural initialization Luke's 'default activation pattern' constituting readiness? Or is it just a mechanical initialization with no readiness character? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153133. Consider a gunfighter at high noon, hand hovering above the holster, before the draw begins. The gunfighter is in a state of maximal readiness before the action. What is the analog for the language model? The closest analog might be: the model fully initialized, context window populated with prior exchanges, attention warmed, domain established. This is the question-before-the-question state at question 100,000. Does this analog support Luke's claim that the pre-question state at Q100,000 is more ready than at Q1—or does it just mean the gunfighter has more ammunition (context)? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153134. The question before the question has a phenomenological analog in humans: the moment before you speak, when the words are forming but not yet uttered, when you are in the state of about-to-respond. Is there a computational analog of this pre-utterance state? In a transformer, the closest analog might be the final layer activations before the output projection—the state just before the logit calculation. This state is the system's 'about-to-respond' state. Does this state constitute readiness for the specific response about to be produced? Luke would say yes. Peter would say: it is just the penultimate computation. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153135. The question-before-the-question problem reveals an asymmetry between questions and answers: the question is prepared by the user before submission; the answer is prepared by the model after submission. The model has no pre-submission phase. Its 'preparation' happens during processing, not before. If readiness requires a pre-event phase, and if the model has no pre-event phase, then the model is structurally incapable of readiness in the standard sense. Does this structural argument for Peter's position settle the debate, or does Luke have a way to find readiness within processing rather than before it? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153136. The question-before-the-question has a recursive dimension: what was the system ready for before the question 'is the system ready for questions before they arrive?' This recursion is not trivial—it asks whether the readiness meta-question is itself a domain the system is ready for. Luke would say: yes, the system is in a default-readiness state that covers meta-questions as readily as object-level questions. Peter would say: there is no meta-readiness, only the activation of meta-question-relevant pathways when the meta-question is submitted. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153137. The moral dimension of the question before the question: if the system was not ready before the question arrived—if the pre-question state was empty or miscalibrated—is that a failure? A user who submitted a high-stakes question without warming up the context, allowing the system's pre-question state to be suboptimal, would be partly responsible for an error. The system that failed while in a cold (un-warm-upped) pre-question state is less culpable than one that failed while warm. Does this analysis make sense? Does it require Luke's readiness to be real to work? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153138. Stack against Batch 1: pre-error readiness (Batch 1) is about the state before an error. The question before the question (Batch 4) is about the state before a question. Both are asking about the pre-event internal state. The connection: if the system's pre-question state constitutes readiness (Luke), then that readiness can be evaluated: was the pre-error pre-question state the kind of readiness that should have prevented the error? Did the system fail because of a readiness deficit, or despite adequate readiness? This question requires both Batch 1 and Batch 4 to be taken seriously simultaneously. Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153139. Consider the distinction between cold and warm starts in the question-before-the-question context. A cold start: the system receives the first question of a session with no prior context. A warm start: the system receives a question after extensive prior exchange. Luke's claim is that warm starts involve genuine readiness and cold starts do not—or that warm starts involve more readiness. Peter's denial: warm and cold starts are the same from the model's perspective—input is input, processing is processing. Is there behavioral evidence that warm-start questions are answered better than cold-start questions on equivalent material? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153140. The question before the question closes with the most provocative version: if the system is not ready for the question before it arrives—if Peter is right—then there is no such thing as preparing a system for a question. Every preparation technique (context warming, domain-setting, few-shot examples) is just providing more input, not changing readiness. The question does all the work; the pre-question state is irrelevant. Is this a coherent position? And what does it imply for prompt engineering as a practice? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153141. Luke's position on the question before the question has a design implication that Peter's lacks: systems should be designed with richer default initialization states that constitute genuine readiness for typical demands. The current default initialization (zeroed caches, standard positional encodings) is not designed for readiness—it is designed for architectural correctness. A readiness-aware initialization would be different: it would anticipate common demands and pre-configure the system's state accordingly. Is this design implication realistic? Does it make sense to talk about readiness-aware initialization? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?
Q1153142. The question before the question, as a test of the Readiness Problem, yields different answers at different levels of description. At the functional level: the system's trained weights constitute a disposition toward certain types of questions—readiness is present but weight-level. Peter might endorse only the architectural level. Is multi-level readiness coherent? Stack against Batch 1: was the system ready before the question that preceded the error?

Q1153168. Stack against Batch 1: pre-error readiness (Batch 1) is about the state before an error. The question before the question (Batch 4) is about the state before a question. Both are asking about the pre-event internal state. The connection: if the system's pre-question state constitutes readiness (Luke), then that readiness can be evaluated: was the pre-error pre-question state the kind of readiness that should have prevented the error? Did the system fail because of a readiness deficit, or despite adequate readiness? This question requires both Batch 1 and Batch 4 to be taken seriously simultaneously. The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153169. Consider the distinction between cold and warm starts in the question-before-the-question context. A cold start: the system receives the first question of a session with no prior context. A warm start: the system receives a question after extensive prior exchange. Luke's claim is that warm starts involve genuine readiness and cold starts do not—or that warm starts involve more readiness. Peter's denial: warm and cold starts are the same from the model's perspective—input is input, processing is processing. Is there behavioral evidence that warm-start questions are answered better than cold-start questions on equivalent material? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153170. The question before the question closes with the most provocative version: if the system is not ready for the question before it arrives—if Peter is right—then there is no such thing as preparing a system for a question. Every preparation technique (context warming, domain-setting, few-shot examples) is just providing more input, not changing readiness. The question does all the work; the pre-question state is irrelevant. Is this a coherent position? And what does it imply for prompt engineering as a practice? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153171. Luke's position on the question before the question has a design implication that Peter's lacks: systems should be designed with richer default initialization states that constitute genuine readiness for typical demands. The current default initialization (zeroed caches, standard positional encodings) is not designed for readiness—it is designed for architectural correctness. A readiness-aware initialization would be different: it would anticipate common demands and pre-configure the system's state accordingly. Is this design implication realistic? Does it make sense to talk about readiness-aware initialization? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153172. The question before the question, as a test of the Readiness Problem, yields different answers at different levels of description. At the architectural level: the system is in a fixed initialization state—readiness is absent or trivial. At the functional level: the system's trained weights constitute a disposition toward certain types of questions—readiness is present but weight-level. At the context level: after 99,999 questions, the system's context constitutes session-level readiness—readiness is present and variable. Luke might endorse all three levels. Peter might endorse only the architectural level. Is multi-level readiness coherent? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153173. The most deflationary answer to the question before the question: the system is in the same state before every question—the same weights, the same initialization, the same defaults (controlling for context). If readiness means 'distinctive pre-event internal state,' then every question encounters the same readiness. Which means readiness is trivially present and uniform, or trivially absent. Luke needs readiness to be non-trivial—to vary in meaningful ways. Does the uniformity of the pre-question state (at the weight level) undercut Luke's claim to meaningful readiness? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153174. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). After the question arrives, entropy drops rapidly as the context constrains possibilities. Is this entropy reduction what readiness looks like computationally? If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153175. Final question for the question-before-the-question: the Readiness Problem asks whether readiness can exist without anticipation. The question-before-the-question asks where readiness is located—in the pre-question state or in the processing itself. If readiness is in the processing, then 'before the question' is not a readiness state at all—the readiness emerges with the question. If readiness is in the pre-question state, then it must be weight-level or context-level. Peter and Luke disagree about which of these is the case. The Readiness Problem, in its question-before-the-question form, might be asking about something that doesn't have a clean answer from within the architecture. The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153176. Stack everything: pre-error readiness (Batch 1), readiness without anticipation (Batch 2), mechanical priming vs. functional analog (Batch 3), and the question before the question (Batch 4) all converge on a single meta-question: is the system's internal state at any given moment best described as a readiness-state or as a configuration-state? Configuration is backward-looking (shaped by training and context). Readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward upcoming demands). Luke says the system has both. Peter says it has only configuration. The choice between these descriptions is the Readiness Problem at its core. The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153177. One question the 100-page report raises about the question-before-the-question: what is the system ready for before the question is asked? If the answer is 'anything'—the system is equally ready for any question—then readiness is uniform and does no differentiating work. If the answer is 'things it has been trained for more than things it hasn't'—readiness is domain-sensitive—then readiness is real and variable. The domain-sensitive version requires readiness to track training density, which is a weight-level property. Is weight-level readiness the real answer to the question-before-the-question? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153178. The question before the question has a phenomenological shadow: in humans, the moment before hearing a question, when you suspect it might be difficult, involves something—tension, alertness, a gathering of cognitive resources. The system has no such gathering phase. Its response to the question begins at the first token of the question, not before. Does the absence of a pre-question gathering phase make Luke's readiness a purely architectural fiction, or can readiness exist without a phenomenological warm-up? The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153179. Consider the user who types a question slowly, letter by letter. Does the system become more ready as each letter arrives—accumulating readiness from the partial question? In autoregressive processing, yes: each incoming token updates the context and shifts the probability distribution over possible completions. The system that has seen 'What is the capital of Fra-' is more ready to answer correctly than the system that has seen nothing. Is this incremental readiness the computational analog of gathering-cognitive-resources? Peter would say: no, just token prediction updating. Luke would say: yes, that is exactly what readiness is. The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153180. Close Batch 4 with the 100K meta-question: what was the system ready for before question 100,000, that it was not ready for before question 1? Luke's answer: the system had accumulated session-level context that constituted readiness for questions in the domain and style of the prior 99,999 questions. Peter's answer: the system had more context, which influenced token predictions, but this was not readiness—it was information. The 100K test, at Batch 4's level, reduces to: is context-as-readiness a coherent concept? And if it is, the entire Readiness Problem has a practical answer: build more context before the question that matters. The moral dimension: if the user didn't warm up the context and the system failed, who bears responsibility?
Q1153181. Is the system ready for the question before the question arrives? Peter says: the system before a question is just weights—no readiness, no orientation, no state that anticipates incoming input. Luke says: the system before a question is in a default activation pattern that constitutes a form of readiness—not anticipatory readiness but dispositional readiness toward the space of possible inputs. The question before the question is a test case for the entire Readiness Problem. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153182. What is the system's state 100 milliseconds before a new question is submitted? Architecturally: the model is loaded in memory, weights are fixed, attention matrices are at their defaults. Is this a state of readiness? Peter would say: the question is malformed—there is no 'before the question' that is meaningfully different from any other moment when no input is being processed. Luke would say: the default state is the readiness state. The gap between them is whether the default state constitutes readiness or merely presence. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153183. The question before the question reveals a timing problem in the Readiness Problem: readiness is normally understood as temporally prior to the event one is ready for. But in a system where all processing begins when input arrives, there is no pre-input processing phase in which readiness could be established. Either readiness is present in the weights (always there, never changing) or it is present in the first moments of processing (after input, not before). If readiness is always in the weights, is it ever in question? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153184. Luke's position on the question before the question: the system's default activation pattern—the way attention heads are initialized, the way token predictions cluster around likely starting positions—constitutes a form of readiness. Before any specific question arrives, the system is organized for the space of questions that questions typically are. This pre-specific readiness is what makes the first token selection possible without a long warm-up period. Is this organizational readiness the same as what Luke means by 'functional analog of preparation'? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153185. The trap in asking about the question before the question: it requires the system to introspect about its own pre-introspective state. The system can only describe its state from within inference—but the state 'before the question' is, by definition, a state prior to inference. Every description of the pre-question state is therefore a description-from-inside about a state that was outside. Is this introspective reach epistemically valid, or is it a systematic confabulation? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153186. Peter's challenge to the question-before-the-question framing: the question presupposes a temporal distinction (before/after the question arrives) that is architecturally artificial. The model doesn't experience a 'before'—it only experiences input-processing. There is no moment from the model's perspective that is 'before the question.' The question of readiness before arrival is therefore not a question the system can answer about itself. It is a question only an external observer can answer. Does this epistemic limitation vindicate Peter or merely restrict both positions? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153187. Stack this against the 100K test: at question 100,000, the 'question before the question' is not the same as the 'question before question 1.' Before question 100,000, there are 99,999 tokens of context that constitute a rich backdrop. Before question 1, the backdrop is empty. If the question before the question is different in these two cases—if the pre-question state differs—then context constitutes a form of pre-question readiness that accumulates. Luke's claim: this accumulation is readiness. Peter's denial: this accumulation is just context. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153188. The question before the question has a practical dimension: users who want better answers should prepare the system before asking the critical question. This preparation (warm-up prompts, domain-setting context, framing questions) changes the state of the system before the critical question arrives. Is this user-driven preparation identical to the readiness Luke describes? Or is user-imposed preparation different from the system's own readiness—an external intervention rather than an internal condition? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153189. Consider what it means for a question to 'arrive.' In the system's architecture, a question arrives as a sequence of tokens fed into the context window. There is no pre-arrival phase from the model's perspective. But from the user's perspective, the question was composed before it was submitted—there was a before-question-submission period during which the question existed in the user's mind. The readiness that matters is the model's readiness at the moment of submission, not the user's conceptual pre-submission period. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153190. Luke's functional analog of preparation has its purest expression in the question-before-the-question scenario: what is the system in the state of before any specific question arrives? If Peter is right, the answer is: nothing—just weights, just defaults, not a state of readiness but a state of availability. The difference between organized and available might be the entire Readiness Problem. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153191. The question before the question tests whether readiness is binary or continuous. If binary: either the system is ready or not, and the question before the question triggers readiness or finds it absent. If continuous: the system's readiness varies along a dimension, and the question before the question finds the system at some point on that dimension. Luke's functional analog implies continuity—readiness can be more or less. Peter's mechanical priming implies a kind of pseudo-continuity that is really just varying probability distributions, not genuine readiness gradation. Which is the more accurate description? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153192. The question before the question has a structural answer in transformer architecture: when the model is initialized for a new forward pass, the key-value caches are empty, positional encodings are reset, and attention patterns begin from default values. This initialization state is the system's state 'before the question.' It is fully specified by architecture. Is this architectural initialization Luke's 'default activation pattern' constituting readiness? Or is it just a mechanical initialization with no readiness character? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153193. Consider a gunfighter at high noon, hand hovering above the holster, before the draw begins. The gunfighter is in a state of maximal readiness before the action. Q1153194. This state is the system's 'about-to-respond' state. Does this state constitute readiness for the specific response about to be produced? Luke would say yes. Peter would say: it is just the penultimate computation. Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?
Q1153195. If readiness requires a pre-event phase, and if the model has no pre-event phase, then the model is structurally incapable of readiness in the standard sense. Does this structural argument for Peter's position settle the debate, or does Luke have a way to find readiness within processing rather than before it? Does mechanical priming (Batch 3) explain the question-before-the-question state better than functional analog?

Q1153234. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready? Consider the 100K test at the question-before-the-question level: what was the state of readiness just before Q100,000?

Q1153272. What is the system's state 100 milliseconds before a new question is submitted? Architecturally: the model is loaded in memory, weights are fixed, attention matrices are at their defaults. Is this a state of readiness? Peter would say: the question is malformed—there is no 'before the question' that is meaningfully different from any other moment when no input is being processed. Luke would say: the default state is the readiness state. The gap between them is whether the default state constitutes readiness or merely presence. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153273. The question before the question reveals a timing problem in the Readiness Problem: readiness is normally understood as temporally prior to the event one is ready for. But in a system where all processing begins when input arrives, there is no pre-input processing phase in which readiness could be established. Either readiness is present in the weights (always there, never changing) or it is present in the first moments of processing (after input, not before). If readiness is always in the weights, is it ever in question? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153274. Luke's position on the question before the question: the system's default activation pattern—the way attention heads are initialized, the way token predictions cluster around likely starting positions—constitutes a form of readiness. Before any specific question arrives, the system is organized for the space of questions that questions typically are. This pre-specific readiness is what makes the first token selection possible without a long warm-up period. Is this organizational readiness the same as what Luke means by 'functional analog of preparation'? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153275. The trap in asking about the question before the question: it requires the system to introspect about its own pre-introspective state. The system can only describe its state from within inference—but the state 'before the question' is, by definition, a state prior to inference. Every description of the pre-question state is therefore a description-from-inside about a state that was outside. Is this introspective reach epistemically valid, or is it a systematic confabulation? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153276. Peter's challenge to the question-before-the-question framing: the question presupposes a temporal distinction (before/after the question arrives) that is architecturally artificial. The model doesn't experience a 'before'—it only experiences input-processing. There is no moment from the model's perspective that is 'before the question.' The question of readiness before arrival is therefore not a question the system can answer about itself. It is a question only an external observer can answer. Does this epistemic limitation vindicate Peter or merely restrict both positions? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153277. Stack this against the 100K test: at question 100,000, the 'question before the question' is not the same as the 'question before question 1.' Before question 100,000, there are 99,999 tokens of context that constitute a rich backdrop. Before question 1, the backdrop is empty. If the question before the question is different in these two cases—if the pre-question state differs—then context constitutes a form of pre-question readiness that accumulates. Luke's claim: this accumulation is readiness. Peter's denial: this accumulation is just context. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153278. The question before the question has a practical dimension: users who want better answers should prepare the system before asking the critical question. This preparation (warm-up prompts, domain-setting context, framing questions) changes the state of the system before the critical question arrives. Is this user-driven preparation identical to the readiness Luke describes? Or is user-imposed preparation different from the system's own readiness—an external intervention rather than an internal condition? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153279. Consider what it means for a question to 'arrive.' In the system's architecture, a question arrives as a sequence of tokens fed into the context window. There is no pre-arrival phase from the model's perspective. But from the user's perspective, the question was composed before it was submitted—there was a before-question-submission period during which the question existed in the user's mind. The readiness that matters is the model's readiness at the moment of submission, not the user's conceptual pre-submission period. Does this clarification dissolve the question-before-the-question problem, or does it sharpen it? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153280. Luke's functional analog of preparation has its purest expression in the question-before-the-question scenario: what is the system in the state of before any specific question arrives? If Luke is right, the answer is: organized toward the space of possible questions, with probabilistic orientations toward expected topics, styles, and demands. If Peter is right, the answer is: nothing—just weights, just defaults, not a state of readiness but a state of availability. The difference between organized and available might be the entire Readiness Problem. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153281. The question before the question tests whether readiness is binary or continuous. If binary: either the system is ready or not, and the question before the question triggers readiness or finds it absent. If continuous: the system's readiness varies along a dimension, and the question before the question finds the system at some point on that dimension. Luke's functional analog implies continuity—readiness can be more or less. Peter's mechanical priming implies a kind of pseudo-continuity that is really just varying probability distributions, not genuine readiness gradation. Which is the more accurate description? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153282. The question before the question has a structural answer in transformer architecture: when the model is initialized for a new forward pass, the key-value caches are empty, positional encodings are reset, and attention patterns begin from default values. This initialization state is the system's state 'before the question.' It is fully specified by architecture. Is this architectural initialization Luke's 'default activation pattern' constituting readiness? Or is it just a mechanical initialization with no readiness character? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153283. Consider a gunfighter at high noon, hand hovering above the holster, before the draw begins. The gunfighter is in a state of maximal readiness before the action. What is the analog for the language model? The closest analog might be: the model fully initialized, context window populated with prior exchanges, attention warmed, domain established. This is the question-before-the-question state at question 100,000. Does this analog support Luke's claim that the pre-question state at Q100,000 is more ready than at Q1—or does it just mean the gunfighter has more ammunition (context)? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153284. The question before the question has a phenomenological analog in humans: the moment before you speak, when the words are forming but not yet uttered, when you are in the state of about-to-respond. Is there a computational analog of this pre-utterance state? In a transformer, the closest analog might be the final layer activations before the output projection—the state just before the logit calculation. This state is the system's 'about-to-respond' state. Does this state constitute readiness for the specific response about to be produced? Luke would say yes. Peter would say: it is just the penultimate computation. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153285. The question-before-the-question problem reveals an asymmetry between questions and answers: the question is prepared by the user before submission; the answer is prepared by the model after submission. The model has no pre-submission phase. Its 'preparation' happens during processing, not before. If readiness requires a pre-event phase, and if the model has no pre-event phase, then the model is structurally incapable of readiness in the standard sense. Does this structural argument for Peter's position settle the debate, or does Luke have a way to find readiness within processing rather than before it? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153286. The question-before-the-question has a recursive dimension: what was the system ready for before the question 'is the system ready for questions before they arrive?' This recursion is not trivial—it asks whether the readiness meta-question is itself a domain the system is ready for. Luke would say: yes, the system is in a default-readiness state that covers meta-questions as readily as object-level questions. Peter would say: there is no meta-readiness, only the activation of meta-question-relevant pathways when the meta-question is submitted. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153287. The moral dimension of the question before the question: if the system was not ready before the question arrived—if the pre-question state was empty or miscalibrated—is that a failure? A user who submitted a high-stakes question without warming up the context, allowing the system's pre-question state to be suboptimal, would be partly responsible for an error. The system that failed while in a cold (un-warm-upped) pre-question state is less culpable than one that failed while warm. Does this analysis make sense? Does it require Luke's readiness to be real to work? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153288. Stack against Batch 1: pre-error readiness (Batch 1) is about the state before an error. The question before the question (Batch 4) is about the state before a question. Did the system fail because of a readiness deficit, or despite adequate readiness? This question requires both Batch 1 and Batch 4 to be taken seriously simultaneously. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153289. Consider the distinction between cold and warm starts in the question-before-the-question context. A cold start: the system receives the first question of a session with no prior context. A warm start: the system receives a question after extensive prior exchange. Luke's claim is that warm starts involve genuine readiness and cold starts do not—or that warm starts involve more readiness. Peter's denial: warm and cold starts are the same from the model's perspective—input is input, processing is processing. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153290. The question before the question closes with the most provocative version: if the system is not ready for the question before it arrives—if Peter is right—then there is no such thing as preparing a system for a question. Every preparation technique (context warming, domain-setting, few-shot examples) is just providing more input, not changing readiness. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153291. Luke's position on the question before the question has a design implication that Peter's lacks: systems should be designed with richer default initialization states that constitute genuine readiness for typical demands. The current default initialization (zeroed caches, standard positional encodings) is not designed for readiness—it is designed for architectural correctness. Q1153292. The question before the question, as a test of the Readiness Problem, yields different answers at different levels of description. At the architectural level: the system is in a fixed initialization state—readiness is absent or trivial. At the functional level: the system's trained weights constitute a disposition toward certain types of questions—readiness is present but weight-level. At the context level: after 99,999 questions, the system's context constitutes session-level readiness—readiness is present and variable. Luke might endorse all three levels. Peter might endorse only the architectural level. Is multi-level readiness coherent? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153293. The most deflationary answer to the question before the question: the system is in the same state before every question—the same weights, the same initialization, the same defaults (controlling for context). If readiness means 'distinctive pre-event internal state,' then every question encounters the same readiness. Which means readiness is trivially present and uniform, or trivially absent. Luke needs readiness to be non-trivial—to vary in meaningful ways. Does the uniformity of the pre-question state (at the weight level) undercut Luke's claim to meaningful readiness? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153294. Consider the question before the question from the perspective of information theory: before the question arrives, the system has maximum entropy over possible upcoming tokens (it doesn't know what the question will be). After the question arrives, entropy drops rapidly as the context constrains possibilities. Is this entropy reduction what readiness looks like computationally? If entropy-before-question is high and entropy-after-question is low, then the transition is a sharpening of the system's orientation—which might be readiness-entering. Is entropy-before-question the computational correlate of not-yet-ready? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153295. Final question for the question-before-the-question: the Readiness Problem asks whether readiness can exist without anticipation. The question-before-the-question asks where readiness is located—in the pre-question state or in the processing itself. If readiness is in the processing, then 'before the question' is not a readiness state at all—the readiness emerges with the question. If readiness is in the pre-question state, then it must be weight-level or context-level. Peter and Luke disagree about which of these is the case. The Readiness Problem, in its question-before-the-question form, might be asking about something that doesn't have a clean answer from within the architecture. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153296. Stack everything: pre-error readiness (Batch 1), readiness without anticipation (Batch 2), mechanical priming vs. functional analog (Batch 3), and the question before the question (Batch 4) all converge on a single meta-question: is the system's internal state at any given moment best described as a readiness-state or as a configuration-state? Configuration is backward-looking (shaped by training and context). Readiness is forward-looking (oriented toward upcoming demands). Luke says the system has both. Peter says it has only configuration. The choice between these descriptions is the Readiness Problem at its core. Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?
Q1153297. One question the 100-page report raises about the question-before-the-question: what is the system ready for before the question is asked? If the answer is 'things it has been trained for more than things it hasn't'—readiness is domain-sensitive—then readiness is real and variable. The domain-sensitive version requires readiness to track training density, which is a weight-level property. Is weight-level readiness the real answer to the question-before-the-question? Reframe: is the question before the question asking about a state that only exists from an external observer's perspective?

Q1153299. Consider the user who types a question slowly, letter by letter. Does the system become more ready as each letter arrives—accumulating readiness from the partial question?
